ScholarshipType: Teaching assistantships, research assistantships, and fellowships

ProgramName: (M.P.A.) in Cornell Institute for Public Affairs
Concentration: Economic and Financial Policy, Environmental Policy, Government, Politics and Policy Studies, Human Rights and Social Justice, International Development Studies, Public and Nonprofit Management, Science, Technology and Infrastructure Policy, Social Policy
Description: The Cornell Institute for Public Affairs (CIPA) offers a two-year graduate program of study leading to the Master of Public Administration (M.P.A.) degree. CIPA’s mission is to provide an outstanding education for those who are committed to public service. CIPA Fellows (our students) develop the knowledge, skills, and personal qualities that are necessary to become effective leaders, analysts, and managers in government, nonprofit organizations, or the private sector. The curriculum is interdisciplinary, rigorous, and flexible. CIPA Fellows study public policy and program management in a global context and learn from a world-class faculty. CIPA Fellows choose from one of eight concentrations: Economic and Financial Policy; Environmental Policy; Government, Politics and Policy Studies; Human Rights and Social Justice; International Development Studies; Public and Nonprofit Management; Science, Technology and Infrastructure Policy; Social Policy. This approach to graduate education gives CIPA Fellows the flexibility to design a program of study that is tailored to their specific interests and long-term career goals. In addition to CIPA courses, students take classes in departments and colleges across Cornell University, including the College of Human Ecology, the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Architecture, Art, and Planning, the College of Arts and Sciences, the School of Industrial and Labor Relations, the Law School, and the Johnson Graduate School of Management.
Accredidation: The Cornell Institute for Public Affairs is accredited by the Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration (NASPAA).

Description: The M.F.A. program in creative writing is a two-year program of intensive work in either poetry or fiction. The program emphasizes the craft of writing and concentrates on the student’s own work. The degree requires six courses, at least four of which must be writing workshops, one of which must be a literature course. In their second year, M.F.A. students teach an introductory creative writing course. All students cap their M.F.A. work with a book-length thesis of either a collection of poems or a collection of short stories or a novel, and a final public reading.

Concentration: Design for Health and Well-being, Sustainable Design Futures, Design Strategy and Innovation
Description: The graduate field of Design and Environmental Analysis (DEA) is dedicated to creating sustainable and healthy futures by design, through leadership in research, education, and outreach. We focus on how the design of the built environment impacts human health and well-being. Using a multidisciplinary, systems view, we integrate knowledge from the design arts, social sciences, and natural sciences to create innovative, sustainable, and healthy design solutions that support individuals, organizations, and communities. DEA offers three graduate degrees: the Ph.D. in Design and Environmental Analysis, the M.S. in Design and Environmental Analysis, and the M.A. in Design and Environmental Analysis.

Concentration: ['Human Centered Design', 'Design for Health and Well-being', 'Sustainable Design Studies']
Description: The graduate field of Design and Environmental Analysis (D+EA) is dedicated to creating sustainable and healthy futures through design, research, and education. Students and faculty in D+EA work to understand how our physical environments affect the way we feel and behave, and what we can do to make them better. Students pursue a master’s or doctoral degree in one of three concentrations: Human Centered Design; Design for Health and Well-being; or Sustainable Design Studies. Each concentration draws upon a multidisciplinary faculty with expertise in human-centered design, environmental psychology, ergonomics, and facility planning and management. Students can also take advantage of D+EA’s extensive resources, including our lighting and acoustics labs and our new state-of-the-art fabrication facilities that enable rapid digital prototyping through 3D printing and laser cutting. Through an interdisciplinary curriculum that includes courses in the social sciences and design, our students develop the skills they need to tackle real-world problems. They graduate from our program ready to work in leading design firms, academic institutions, and public and private organizations across the globe.

Concentration: ['Design Innovation and Strategy', 'Sustainable Design Studies', 'Human Centered Design']
Description: The graduate field of Design and Environmental Analysis (D+EA) focuses on design research, the creation of sustainable and healthy futures, and the study of the near environment and its occupants. The field’s multidisciplinary faculty have expertise in human-centered design, environmental psychology, ergonomics, facility planning and management, and sustainable design. Students work with their Special Committee to define a specific course of study and research problem. The Ph.D. program prepares students for careers in academia, research, or consulting.
ScholarshipType: Teaching assistantships (TAs), Research assistantships (RAs), and Fellowships

Description: The Design + Technology M.S. program is a one-year, two-semester program at Cornell Tech in New York City. This is an intensive, multi-disciplinary program that blends research, artistry, critical thinking, and technical innovation. Throughout the program, students work in teams with students from other Cornell Tech programs on real-world challenges posed by businesses, institutions, and community groups in the Studio curriculum.
ScholarshipType: Fellowships, assistantships, travel grants, and loans

Description: The Master of Science (M.S.) in Design Technology is a two-year post-professional degree that is open to applicants who hold a first professional degree in a design field such as architecture, landscape architecture, urban design, etc., or an undergraduate degree in a related field such as computer science, engineering, art, science, or humanities. The program is specifically focused on developing critical and robust research projects that use emergent technology in a creative and speculative manner. Students are encouraged to develop a unique research trajectory that culminates in a master’s thesis. The program draws on the rich multidisciplinary environment at Cornell to build a course of study that is tailored to each student’s particular interest. All students in the program are required to participate in the departmental teaching program.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: International, national, and local development processes, Population and environment, Social inequality
Description:
The graduate field of development sociology at Cornell is widely recognized as a leader in its field. The M.S. and Ph.D. programs offer a combination of strong disciplinary training in sociology and broad interdisciplinary study of the social, political, economic, and cultural processes that shape development.

Students may emphasize any of several areas of study:

- international, national, and local development processes
- inequality
- population and environment

The field provides opportunities for study and research in major areas of the world—Africa, Asia, Europe, and North and Latin America. Training can include instruction in appropriate foreign languages, econometrics and other advanced quantitative methods, qualitative methods, and geographic information systems. A major strength of the program is the opportunity for students to work closely with a Special Committee of faculty members chosen by the student to represent his or her major and minor fields of study. Faculty members in the field are associated with the Department of Development Sociology and other departments in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and other colleges at Cornell.
ScholarshipType: Fellowships, Assistantships, Travel Grants, Conference Grants

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Population and Development', 'States, Markets, and Institutions', 'Sociology of Development']
Description:
The graduate field of development sociology has a long and distinguished history of research, teaching, and service around the world. Faculty are committed to engaged research that addresses major global challenges. With a strong tradition of international and domestic research, development sociology is concerned with the causes and consequences of social and economic change, and the linkages of the local and the global. Specific faculty research interests include a range of topics in the areas of international and domestic development, demography, environment and natural resources, and rural and agricultural change. Research and teaching are organized around three concentrations: 1) states, markets, and institutions; 2) population and development; and 3) sociology of development. Faculty also direct the Community and Regional Development Institute (CaRDI) and are affiliated with several area studies programs.

The field offers a Ph.D. in development sociology. The Ph.D. program is research-oriented, and students work closely with faculty in their areas of specialization. The program provides strong training in sociological theory and research methods as they apply to development studies. Most students conduct field research for their dissertations, and the program has an excellent record of placing its graduates in academic and research positions in the U.S. and around the world. For students seeking a practice-oriented degree, the Department of Global Development offers a professional master’s degree program (M.P.S.) in global development.

Department: College of Arts and Sciences; College of Human Ecology
Concentration: Developmental Psychology
Description: The graduate field of human development offers M.A., M.S., and Ph.D. degree programs that provide an in-depth understanding of human development from a variety of disciplinary and methodological perspectives. The field uses a life-course perspective to understand human development in diverse contexts and settings. Research strengths in the field include the following: the cognitive, social, emotional, and biological aspects of development; the influence of social and cultural contexts (e.g., family, peers, school, community, culture) on development; and the role of developmental processes in the etiology of psychopathology, risk, and resilience. Students also have opportunities for direct experience with research and practice in applied settings, such as the Bronfenbrenner Center for Translational Research.
AverageScholarshipAmount: All admitted Ph.D. students receive a funding package which includes a stipend (the 9-month stipend for 2024-2025 is $43,146), full tuition, and health insurance.
ScholarshipAmount: All admitted Ph.D. students receive a funding package which includes a stipend (the 9-month stipend for 2024-2025 is $43,146), full tuition, and health insurance.

Description: Developmental psychology is the scientific study of how and why individuals change over the course of their lives. Originally concerned with infants and children, the field has expanded to include adolescence, adult development, aging, and the entire lifespan. This field examines change across a broad range of topics including motor skills and other psycho-physiological processes; cognitive development involving areas such as problem solving, moral understanding, and conceptual understanding; language acquisition; social, personality, and emotional development; and self-concept and identity formation. Students are also encouraged to participate in one or more of the several interdisciplinary programs on campus, including the Cognitive Studies Program and the Cornell Institute for Public Affairs. Close ties are maintained with faculty members in other fields, including those in the other psychology departments, Human Development, Neurobiology and Behavior, and the Division of Nutritional Sciences. Faculty and students often collaborate with colleagues from the Weill Cornell Medical College.

The graduate field of East Asian literature offers a program of study leading to the Ph.D. degree. The field brings together faculty and graduate students with shared interests in the literary traditions of China, Japan, and Korea from the classical and modern periods. The field is committed to the study of East Asian literature from a variety of theoretical and interdisciplinary perspectives in a comparatist framework. Training is offered in the literary traditions of China, Japan, and Korea. Students are expected to achieve a high level of competence in at least one East Asian language. They are admitted to study in the field of East Asian literature as a whole, and declare a major and two minor areas of concentration at the end of their first year of study. Possible major concentrations are Chinese literature, Japanese literature, and Korean literature. Minor concentrations are chosen from a list of options that includes a second East Asian literature, as well as a range of other possibilities such as anthropology, art history, comparative literature, feminist, gender & sexuality studies, film, history, linguistics, performing and media arts, and religious studies. In all cases, a student’s course of study is organized in close consultation with the Special Committee. The program of study is administered by the Department of Asian Studies.
AverageScholarshipAmount: Guaranteed funding package for five years including full tuition, a stipend, and health insurance. The 9-month minimum stipend for 2024-25 is $34,064.
ScholarshipAmount: Guaranteed funding package for five years including full tuition, a stipend, and health insurance. The 9-month minimum stipend for 2024-25 is $34,064.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: Animal Behavior, Biogeochemistry, Community and Ecosystem Ecology, Ecological and Evolutionary Genomics and Genetics, Evolutionary Patterns and Processes, Organismal Biology, Plant-Animal Interactions, Population and Evolutionary Ecology, Sustainable Development
Description:
The graduate field of ecology and evolutionary biology is a large, diverse, and collaborative group of faculty and graduate students studying a wide range of topics and organisms in ecology and evolutionary biology. Students in the graduate program in EEB may pursue studies at the M.S. or Ph.D. level. Students are trained in the broad disciplines of ecology and evolutionary biology. They learn the fundamentals of the scientific process from the generation of research questions and hypotheses to the design of empirical studies and the analysis and interpretation of data. Students are exposed to the breadth of research in ecology and evolutionary biology through seminars and journal clubs and become experts in their own research areas.

The Field of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology offers M.S. and Ph.D. degrees. The M.S. degree is generally awarded to students as a step toward earning a Ph.D., and very few students are admitted to the field for a terminal M.S. degree. Prospective M.S. students are encouraged to contact EEB faculty to inquire about opportunities in their labs.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: Animal Behavior, Chemical Ecology, Community and Ecosystem Ecology, Environmental and Organismal Biology, Evolutionary Genetics and Genomics, Evolutionary Patterns and Processes, Plant Biology, Sustainable Development
Description:
The graduate field of ecology and evolutionary biology includes more than 100 faculty from 17 departments in six colleges, plus the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and the Boyce Thompson Institute. We are united by an interest in ecology and evolution and a desire to train the next generation of leaders in these areas. The field is broadly organized into eight graduate concentrations: Animal Behavior; Chemical Ecology; Community and Ecosystem Ecology; Environmental and Organismal Biology; Evolutionary Genetics and Genomics; Evolutionary Patterns and Processes; Plant Biology; and Sustainable Development. Each is an intellectual hub for faculty and students with shared interests. Most faculty and students identify with more than one concentration.

Students may pursue either a M.S. or a Ph.D. degree. The Ph.D. is a research degree requiring an original contribution to science. The M.S. is also a research degree; it may be an appropriate goal for students who have not had a great deal of research experience, or for students whose career plans require a M.S. but not a Ph.D.

All students work closely with a Special Committee of three or four faculty members who help guide the student’s graduate education and research. The committee must include at least one member from each of two graduate concentrations. One member of the committee may be from outside the field of EEB. Students also may have an unofficial advisor on their committee from a cooperating institution, such as the American Museum of Natural History.

Most graduate students in the field of ecology and evolutionary biology receive financial support in the form of fellowships, research assistantships, and/or teaching assistantships. The support package includes tuition, a stipend, and health insurance.
ScholarshipAmount: Full tuition plus a minimum stipend of $43,126 per year
ScholarshipType: Fellowships, teaching assistantships (TAs), and graduate research assistantships (GRAs)

Department: College of Arts & Sciences and College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: Behavioral Economics, Contract Theory and Information Economics, Econometrics, Economic Development, Economic History, Economic Theory, Industrial Organization, International Economics, Labor Economics, Political Economy, Public Economics
Description:
The graduate program in economics at Cornell is a Ph.D. program that trains students to be leaders in economic research. Cornell’s Ph.D. program in economics is a research degree and is usually pursued by students who wish to do the kind of research done by academic economists.

The doctoral program in economics has two stages. The first is a two-year sequence of courses that provides rigorous training in economic theory and econometrics. In this period, students acquire the essential tools to do economic research. Students must pass comprehensive examinations in microeconomics and macroeconomics at the end of their first year and an econometrics comprehensive exam at the beginning of their second year. After successfully completing two years of course work, students are admitted to candidacy for the Ph.D. degree.

The second stage of the program is the thesis, or dissertation, which is a significant piece of independent research. In this stage, the student works closely with his or her Special Committee. Students are required to present a research paper (known as the “A Exam” or Admission to Candidacy Examination) in their third year of study. They must complete the dissertation and defend it in an oral examination (the “B Exam”). The final examination is an oral defense of the thesis. Most students complete their doctoral studies in five years.
ScholarshipAmount: $43,730 stipend per year plus tuition and health insurance

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: Educational Psychology and Human Development, Learning, Cognition, and Development, Research, Evaluation, and Measurement, Social and Cultural Foundations of Education
Description: The graduate field of education provides advanced study for those who want to contribute to the improvement of education. Disciplinary foundations come primarily from psychology, sociology, and philosophy. Students acquire a broad understanding of the educational enterprise as well as deep knowledge in their chosen concentration. The program is flexible and individualized, with students working closely with their Special Committee. Special Committee members are chosen from the faculty of the field of education and one member must be chosen from a graduate field outside of education.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS)
Concentration: Educational Psychology and Human Development; Learning, Cognition, and Development; or Social and Cultural Foundations of Education
Description: The graduate field of education offers two degrees: a master of science (M.S.) and a doctor of philosophy (Ph.D.). These degree programs prepare graduates for careers as researchers in academic or other settings and for leadership positions in educational systems and related social institutions. The M.S. degree is a research-focused degree, designed for students interested in developing research skills; it is not a teacher certification program. Students choose from one of three concentrations: Educational Psychology and Human Development; Learning, Cognition, and Development; or Social and Cultural Foundations of Education.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Curriculum and Instruction', 'Educational Psychology and Human Development', 'Learning, Cognition, and Development', 'Research, Evaluation, and Measurement', 'Science Education']
Description: The graduate field of education addresses the role of education in a democratic and multicultural society. Its central mission is to advance knowledge about learning and teaching in a variety of social settings. Cornell’s graduate field of education is interdisciplinary. This characteristic makes the field especially well-suited for preparing scholars, researchers and practitioners who can respond to the challenges of education in the 21st century.
ScholarshipType: Fellowships, Teaching Assistantships (TAs), Research Assistantships (RAs), and Graduate Assistantships (GAs)

Concentration: ['Computer Engineering & Digital Systems (COMP)', 'Information, Communication, & Network Theory (ICN)', 'Solid-State Devices, Electronics, & Photonics (SSEP)', 'Biomedical Imaging, Bioelectrical Engineering & Nanosystems (BION)', 'Energy Systems & Power Electronics (ESPE)', 'Signal, Sensor, & Data Sciences (SSDS)', 'Physics of ECE Devices, Systems, & Information (PEDS)']
Description: The graduate field of Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) offers a research-oriented M.S./Ph.D. program in which students can pursue studies in a broad range of topics. The M.S. degree requires a thesis and prepares students for advanced research and development positions. Students in the ECE M.S./Ph.D. program have a great deal of flexibility in creating a course of study that is tailored to their particular interests. Research is an essential part of the M.S. degree and is conducted under the supervision of a faculty advisor. M.S./Ph.D. students typically receive financial support in the form of a fellowship, a research assistantship, or a teaching assistantship.

Concentration: ['Bio-Electrical Engineering', 'Computer Engineering', 'Data Science', 'Electrical Engineering Systems', 'Energy Systems', 'Information, Communication and Decision Theory', 'Integrated Circuits and VLSI', 'Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS)', 'Optics and Photonics', 'Physics of Semiconductor Devices', 'Quantum Information Processing', 'Robotics', 'Signal Processing', 'Solid-State Devices', 'Space Tech']
Description: The graduate field of electrical and computer engineering offers a broad, flexible program of study leading to the Cornell degrees of Master of Engineering (M.Eng.), Master of Science (M.S.), and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.). ECE at Cornell is consistently ranked among the top electrical and computer engineering departments in the world. As a Ph.D. student, you will have the opportunity to work with world-renowned faculty on research projects at the forefront of innovation. Our students are among the most sought-after in the world by leading academic institutions, industrial research labs, and corporations. The Ph.D. degree is a research-based degree that requires an original contribution to the field of electrical and computer engineering. Ph.D. students pursue a major and two minors and must pass a comprehensive examination in their chosen area of study. The minors can be chosen from any field in the university, which offers Ph.D. students the ability to pursue a wide range of interdisciplinary degrees.

The Master of Engineering (M.Eng.) degree in Engineering Management is a career-focused graduate degree designed to develop leaders in engineering and technology. The program provides a strong foundation in management fundamentals in the context of engineering and technology, combined with an ability to apply these concepts in practice. The curriculum develops management and leadership skills, including communication, ethics, and teamwork, and provides an opportunity to develop depth in a particular area of interest or breadth across a range of technical and managerial areas.

Concentration: ['American studies', 'Feminist, gender, and sexuality studies', 'Lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender studies', 'Medieval studies', 'Visual studies', 'Film and video studies', 'Africana studies', 'Asian American studies', 'American Indian and Indigenous studies', 'Latina/o studies']
Description: The graduate program in English at Cornell has long been recognized as one of the best in the country, and we are committed to keeping it that way. We have a large and diverse graduate faculty with a wide range of theoretical and critical interests. The graduate program includes about 60 students in the Ph.D. program and another 12 in the M.F.A. program in Creative Writing. We offer a fully-funded Ph.D. program that admits 8-10 students a year with a six-year package of support. A relatively small program, we pride ourselves on a consistent record of placing our students in academic positions. Our program has been ranked among the top programs by the National Research Council (NRC). The field has strengths in all of the traditional historical periods of English and American literature. At the same time, we have a strong and growing commitment to the fields of post-colonial studies, minority literatures, and cultural studies. Students can take courses in and work with faculty in other departments such as Comparative Literature, the Society for the Humanities, Romance Studies, German Studies, Government, History, and History of Art, as well as in interdisciplinary programs such as Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies; Medieval Studies; and Visual Culture. Close interaction among faculty and students is a key feature of our program; a lively conference and colloquium series as well as more informal events provide a sense of intellectual community. We encourage you to contact faculty in your fields of interest. We invite you to experience the intellectual excitement and rigor of a first-rate graduate program.

The field of entomology has a long and distinguished history at Cornell, beginning with the appointment of John Henry Comstock in 1872. Today, the field includes more than 30 faculty members from the departments of Entomology, Neurobiology and Behavior, Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, and Molecular Biology and Genetics. The field has particular strength in the areas of systematics and evolutionary biology, ecology, behavior, chemical ecology, molecular entomology and genomics, insect pathology, integrated pest management, medical and veterinary entomology, and apiculture. Facilities include the Cornell University Insect Collection, with more than 7 million specimens; the Page Honey Bee Research Laboratory; modern laboratories for research in all aspects of entomology; an extensive entomological library; and access to a variety of natural areas for field research. Graduate students are encouraged to select a research topic prior to or shortly after arrival on campus and to select a Special Committee of three or four faculty members that represents the student’s specific interests. Students are admitted to the field and not to the laboratory of an individual faculty member. Funding in the form of teaching or research assistantships or fellowships is available to most students.

Concentration: Acarology, Apiculture, Arthropod Pathology, Biological Control, Chemical Ecology, Insect Biochemistry and Toxicology, Insect Ecology, Insect Morphology, Insect Systematics, Insect-Plant Interactions, Integrated Pest Management, Medical and Veterinary Entomology, Molecular and Genetic Entomology, Urban Entomology
Description: The graduate field of entomology offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs that provide advanced training in a major area of specialization within the entomological sciences. Because of the great diversity of insects and their activities, the field is subdivided into several major areas of specialization: acarology; apiculture; arthropod pathology; biological control; chemical ecology; medical and veterinary entomology; molecular and genetic entomology; insect morphology; insect ecology; insect-plant interactions; insect biochemistry and toxicology; insect systematics; integrated pest management; and urban entomology. Students identify a special committee of three or four faculty members who represent their major and minor areas of study, guide their academic and research programs, and administer their examinations.

ProgramName: (M.S./Ph.D.) in Environmental and Water Resources Systems Engineering
Concentration: Environmental and Water Resources Systems Engineering
Description: Study and research in this area are directed toward the development and application of mathematical models for the planning, design, and operation of water resource and environmental systems. Students are encouraged to develop a firm background in the underlying physical, chemical, and biological sciences and in the analytic methods of systems engineering, including optimization, simulation, and statistical analysis. Some current research projects include: optimal design and operation of water quality and quantity control systems; analysis of environmental policy and regulation; and application of expert systems to environmental and water resource problems. Research opportunities also exist for collaborative work with other divisions of the University, such as the Center for Applied Mathematics, the Program of Computer Graphics, the Theory Center, the School of Operations Research and Industrial Engineering, and the Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering. Graduates in this area are prepared for careers in teaching, research, consulting, and government in the public and private sectors.

ProgramName: (M.A.) in Fiber Science and Apparel Design
Concentration: ['Fiber Science', 'Apparel Design']
Description: The graduate field of Fiber Science and Apparel Design (FSAD) is composed of faculty members from the College of Human Ecology. The field offers M.A., M.S. and Ph.D. degrees with a major in Fiber Science or Apparel Design. The field also offers a M.P.S. degree in Human Ecology. Graduate studies in FSAD integrate knowledge from the physical and social sciences as well as art and design to create innovative and sustainable solutions that address the needs of the individual, family, and society. The field offers a multidisciplinary program with strong roots in polymer science, engineering, chemistry, physics, materials science, anthropology, economics, sociology, design, and art. Modern, well-equipped laboratories with state-of-the-art instruments are available for research.

ProgramName: (M.S.) in Fiber Science and Apparel Design
Concentration: ['Apparel Design', 'Fiber and Polymer Science', 'Human Centered Design']
Description: The field of Fiber Science and Apparel Design offers M.S. and Ph.D. degrees with concentrations in: Apparel Design; Fiber and Polymer Science; and Human Centered Design. Research in the field focuses on the use of apparel design, fibers, and textiles to meet human needs. Research combines the pure and applied sciences with design, creativity, and technology. Current research topics include: design processes for functional and expressive apparel and other products, including design for specific user groups, and the integration of smart technologies in textile-based products; the engineering of fibrous materials for a variety of end uses; the study of polymeric materials for fiber applications including biopolymers and green composites; the investigation of sustainable practices for the apparel and textile industry; and historical and cultural aspects of textiles and apparel.

ProgramName: (Ph.D.) in Fiber Science and Apparel Design
Concentration: ['Fiber Science', 'Textile Technology', 'Apparel Design']
Description:
The graduate field of Fiber Science and Apparel Design (FSAD) leads to M.S. and Ph.D. degrees and prepares students for careers in academia, government, and industry. In both programs, students choose a major subject area and two minor subjects. Study in the field of FSAD offers a unique experience integrating design, art, biology, chemistry, engineering, and social sciences to address emerging challenges in the field of textiles and apparel. The field has three major areas of specialization: fiber science, textile technology, and apparel design.

In addition, the field offers a master of professional studies (M.P.S.) in Human Ecology. This one-year, course-based master’s degree prepares individuals for leadership roles in various professions. Students complete a capstone project in lieu of a research thesis.

Cornell is an internationally recognized leader in the field of fiber science. Research encompasses the study of the physical and chemical properties of fibrous materials, the development of new fibers and fibrous systems, and the application of new technologies to the creation of innovative materials and products.

The study of apparel design focuses on the complex process by which apparel products are conceived, produced, and marketed in the context of a global fashion industry. Graduate student research in this area explores the artistic, technical, and social aspects of apparel design and product development.

Concentration: food science, food technology
Description: The graduate field of food science and technology offers studies leading to M.S., M.F.S. (Master of Food Science), and Ph.D. degrees. The M.F.S. degree is a one-year, course-work-only master's degree program that does not require a research thesis. A wide range of courses are offered to provide a strong foundation in the basic sciences and to allow for specialization. Students can select a concentration in food science or food technology. Research programs are available in food chemistry, food microbiology, food engineering, food processing, dairy science, enology, food quality, sensory evaluation, food toxicology, and international food science.

Concentration: ['Dairy Science', 'Enology', 'Food Chemistry', 'Food Engineering', 'Food Microbiology', 'Food Processing Waste Technology', 'International Food Science', 'Sensory Evaluation']
Description: The M.S. degree program in food science and technology is a research-based degree that requires a thesis. Students take a minimum of 2 of the following 4 core courses: Food Chemistry, Food Microbiology, Food Engineering, and Sensory Evaluation. Students also take statistics and seminar courses. The remaining courses are chosen by the student in consultation with his or her Special Committee. Students are required to serve as teaching assistants for at least one semester. Most students with an M.S. degree find professional positions in the food industry or in government.

Concentration: ['Dairy Science', 'Enology', 'Food Chemistry', 'Food Engineering', 'Food Microbiology', 'Food Processing Waste Technology', 'Food Quality', 'International Food Science', 'Sensory Evaluation']
Description: The graduate field of food science and technology provides an opportunity for graduate study in a wide range of areas related to the science of food. The field offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs and a one-year M.F.S. (master of food science) degree program. Concentrations include food chemistry, food microbiology, food engineering, food processing waste technology, sensory evaluation, enology, dairy science, food quality, and international food science.

Concentration: ['Developmental Biology', 'Evolutionary Genetics and Genomics', 'Genetics and Genomics', 'Molecular and Cell Biology', 'Systems and Computational Biology', 'Vertebrate Genomics']
Description: The graduate field of genetics, genomics and development (GGD) is composed of 50 faculty members from 11 departments in five colleges at the Ithaca campus and the Medical College in New York City. The research interests of the GGD faculty span the breadth of modern genetics and genomics, including the areas of molecular genetics, developmental genetics, evolutionary genetics, population genetics, computational genetics, and genomics. The organisms under study include viruses, bacteria, protists, fungi, plants, and animals (including humans). GGD is a diverse and exciting field that provides unusually broad research and training opportunities. A common theme in the field of GGD is the use of genetic, genomic, and developmental approaches to understand fundamental biological questions. The field’s major strengths lie in the study of developmental genetics, evolutionary genetics and genomics, and systems biology.

Concentration: genetics and genomics; developmental biology; and computational and statistical genomics
Description: The graduate field of genetics, genomics and development (GGD) is a campus-wide community of faculty and graduate students with primary research interests in the areas of genetics, genomics, molecular, cellular, and developmental biology. The field brings together faculty from several colleges and departments to create a collaborative and supportive research and training environment. The primary objective of the field is to provide a training program that is flexible and tailored to the individual needs of students who wish to pursue a research career in these disciplines. Students affiliate with a particular concentration by their second year of study. Concentrations include genetics and genomics; developmental biology; and computational and statistical genomics. The GGD curriculum is similarly flexible to accommodate students with diverse interests. In the first year, students take courses and carry out three rotations in different faculty laboratories to find the ideal match for their interests. Throughout their time in the program, students take additional specialized courses related to their research, have opportunities to assist with undergraduate teaching, and participate in a rich environment of weekly seminar series, journal clubs, and retreats. Students are also encouraged to travel to national and international meetings, as well as other scientific conferences where they present their work.

The graduate field of geological sciences is composed of faculty from the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. Research in geological sciences at Cornell covers a wide spectrum, ranging from the deep earth to its surface and from billion-year-old rocks to active volcanoes. Cornell geoscientists are engaged in research all over the world, with especially active programs in the Andes, the Pacific, the Caribbean, the Middle East, and the American West. Graduate study in geology, geobiology, geophysics, geochemistry, and geohydrology is conducted in a stimulating atmosphere of departmental seminars, informal discussion groups, and close student-faculty interaction.

Concentration: ['Geophysics', 'Geochemistry/Petrology', 'Structural Geology', 'Sedimentology', 'Paleontology', 'Oceanography', 'Geobiology', 'Geohydrology', 'Planetary Science', 'Economic Geology', 'Environmental Geosciences']
Description: The graduate field of geological sciences at Cornell has a distinguished history of leadership in research and education, and our current graduate program reflects a special strength in the interdisciplinary approach to geological and geophysical problems. Research areas include geophysics, geochemistry, structural geology, sedimentology, marine geology, petroleum geology, paleontology, and mineral physics.

Concentration: Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, Film and Video Studies, Jewish Studies, Medieval and Early Modern Studies, Performing and Media Arts, Visual Studies
Description: The Field of Germanic Studies offers a doctor of philosophy (Ph.D.) degree. The program provides a flexible and supportive environment for students who are eager to become accomplished scholars and teachers of German literature and culture. Graduate students in Germanic Studies are offered courses and individual guidance in literary history and theory, cultural studies, intellectual history and philosophy, gender studies, film and media studies, Jewish studies, and other areas of German culture from the early modern period to the present.

Concentration: Social justice and equity, Environment and sustainability, Economic and development policy, Agriculture, food systems and rural development, Community, learning and development, Development strategy and evaluation
Description: The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Global Development is an interdisciplinary, one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares individuals for careers in international development. Through a combination of coursework and an intensive, hands-on capstone project, you’ll develop the knowledge and skills to lead change, create more equitable and sustainable communities and make a difference in the world. As a student in our program, you will join a diverse cohort of experienced professionals and emerging leaders from around the globe. Coursework will equip you with a foundational understanding of development theory, policy and practice, as well as specialized knowledge in your chosen concentration area. The main objective of our M.P.S. program is to train skilled, thoughtful and effective development practitioners who are equipped to address the world’s most pressing challenges. Our program provides a solid foundation for careers in a wide range of fields, including international agriculture and rural development, community and economic development, development policy, social justice and equity, environmental protection and program planning, management and evaluation.

Concentration: ['Development Sociology', 'International Agriculture and Rural Development']
Description:
The graduate field of global development offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs that are broadly concerned with the challenges of international development. Within the M.S. degree program, students specialize in either Development Sociology or International Agriculture and Rural Development. Students interested in the Ph.D. program should refer to the graduate field of development sociology.

Students take a multidisciplinary approach to the study of social, political, economic, and environmental change in the global South. The program offers a strong theoretical and research-based course of study and prepares students for careers in research, policy analysis, and university-level teaching.

Students who elect to study Development Sociology are asked to concentrate in one of the following areas: states, markets, and institutions, or social and political change. Within those areas, students may choose to focus on a particular topic such as community and local development, gender, political economy, population and development, rural sociology, or environment and development. Students choosing to study International Agriculture and Rural Development are encouraged to combine interests in the social sciences with a strong grounding in at least one technical field related to agriculture and rural development.

Concentration: ['Development policy and practice', 'Development sociology', 'International agriculture and rural development', 'International nutrition']
Description: The graduate field of global development is a premier, world-renowned center for research and graduate training on processes of social, economic, political, and environmental change at the local, national and global scales. The field is problem-focused, interdisciplinary, and empirically-grounded, with a particular emphasis on the challenges of development in the Global South. Faculty affiliated with the field are drawn from a wide range of disciplines across the social and natural sciences. Students pursuing a Ph.D. in global development must complete a major in development sociology and may choose a minor from one of the other three concentrations in the field or from one of the many other graduate fields at Cornell. The field offers four concentrations: development policy and practice; development sociology; international agriculture and rural development; and international nutrition. Most students complete a significant part of their dissertation research outside the United States; research may be undertaken on the Cornell campus or at one of our many international partner institutions.

Concentration: ['American Politics', 'Comparative Politics', 'International Relations', 'Political Methodology', 'Political Theory']
Description: The graduate program in government is designed to train students for careers in research and teaching. The program is small, selective, and emphasizes close contact between faculty and graduate students. Students normally enter the program with the intention of earning a Ph.D. degree. The program provides a broad education in the substance and methods of political science, and it supports students to develop their own specialized research agendas. The faculty’s research interests are highly diverse and interdisciplinary, and students can find support for a wide range of research projects. The field has particular strengths in American politics, comparative politics, political theory and international relations. Its faculty also have expertise in a wide range of interdisciplinary areas, such as political economy, political behavior, law and politics, and race and ethnicity.

Concentration: ['preservation planning', 'historic conservation', 'real estate']
Description: The graduate field of Historic Preservation Planning (HPP) offers a two-year master of arts (M.A.) degree. HPP is the only historic preservation program in the United States that is part of a department of city and regional planning and a college of architecture, art, and planning. As a result, the field takes a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach to preservation that encompasses history and theory, planning, conservation, design, economics, law, and technology. The program offers students the opportunity to learn from and work with faculty members who have expertise in a broad range of related areas, including architectural conservation, preservation planning, landscape preservation, urban history, and real estate. Students may earn a concentration in either preservation planning, historic conservation, or real estate.

Concentration: ['African History', 'American History', 'Ancient Greek History', 'Ancient Roman History', 'Early Modern European History', 'English History', 'French History', 'German History', 'History of Science', 'Italian History', 'Japanese History', 'Latin American History', 'Medieval Chinese History', 'Medieval European History', 'Modern Chinese History', 'Modern European History', 'Russian History', 'Southeast Asian History']
Description: The graduate program in history is designed to train students for careers in research and teaching at the university and college levels and for careers as public historians in government service, museums, and archives. The program requires all students to develop a major field of study, which usually means preparation for both teaching and research in a specific chronological and geographical area. Students also normally prepare two minor fields, one of which must be in an area of history outside the major field and the other of which may be in another discipline (such as art history, government, or classics). Some major fields require specific minor fields.

ProgramName: (Ph.D.) in History of Art and Archaeology
Concentration: ['African American Art', 'African Art', 'American Art', 'Ancient Art and Archaeology', 'Baroque Art', 'East Asian Art', 'Eighteenth-Century Art', 'Latin American Art', 'Medieval Art', 'Modern and Contemporary Art', 'Nineteenth-Century Art', 'Renaissance Art', 'South Asian Art', 'Southeast Asian Art', 'Visual Culture']
Description: The graduate program in the History of Art and Archaeology is designed to provide students with a comprehensive knowledge of the history, theory, and criticism of art. While working closely with their advisors, students have the opportunity to take seminars with a wide range of faculty members whose interests cover diverse areas of art history, visual culture, and archaeology. The department encourages students to develop a course of study that reflects their specific intellectual interests, and to take courses in other departments and programs.

Concentration: Horticultural Biology, Horticultural Crop Production Systems, Public Garden Leadership
Description: The graduate field of horticulture is a multi-disciplinary program that addresses the art, science, technology, and business of plant cultivation. As a horticulture graduate student at Cornell, you will be well-positioned to tackle complex agricultural challenges including food and nutritional security, health and well-being, and environmental sustainability. From developing new fruit and vegetable varieties to managing landscapes and turfgrass, from creating better production systems for food and ornamental crops to improving post-harvest handling and storage, our faculty are leaders in their disciplines and work at the cutting-edge of plant science research. Our faculty are based in the School of Integrative Plant Science on the Ithaca campus, and at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, NY. Students can select from a diversity of research topics including plant breeding and genetics, genomics, plant physiology, controlled environment agriculture (CEA), public garden leadership, international agriculture, post-harvest biology, turfgrass science, and production, marketing, and business management of horticultural crops. Research may be conducted in labs, greenhouses, farms, or with communities, in both local and global settings. Our graduates go on to successful careers in academia, industry, government, and for non-profit organizations in the U.S. and around the world.

Concentration: ['Horticultural Plant Breeding and Genetics', 'Horticultural Plant Physiology and Ecology', 'Horticultural Crop Production and Management']
Description: The graduate field of horticulture provides an integrated course of study in the biology and technology of horticultural crops (fruits, vegetables, and landscape plants). The graduate faculty has expertise in a wide range of disciplines that span the biological and environmental sciences. Research areas include plant breeding and genetics, genomics, plant physiology, plant-microbe interactions, postharvest biology, sustainable and organic production systems, and controlled-environment agriculture. Students have access to outstanding research facilities, including state-of-the-art laboratories and growth chambers, extensive germplasm collections, and several research farms.

Concentration: Aging & Health; Cognitive Development; Law, Psychology, & Human Development; Social & Personality Development
Description: The graduate field of Human Development offers M.A. and Ph.D. degree programs that focus on the psychological, social, and biological development of people and families across the life-span. Students in human development have excellent opportunities to form interdisciplinary collaborations with faculty and other students throughout the College of Human Ecology and Cornell University, including those in the fields of psychology, sociology, and neurobiology and behavior, as well as the Cornell Law School, and Weill Cornell Medical College. All students receive a strong theoretical and methodological grounding to do their research in one or more of the core areas of developmental psychology. In addition, students have the opportunity to take part in two training grants: one on the developmental psychobiology of stress and one on aging.

ProgramName: (Ph.D.) in Human Development and Family Studies
Concentration: Aging and Health; Cognitive Development; Developmental Behavioral Neuroscience; Law and Human Development; Social and Personality Development
Description: The graduate field of human development offers a Ph.D. program that gives students a strong foundation in the theories and research of human development while also allowing them to specialize in an area of their own interest. Students are admitted to the field of human development as a whole, rather than to a particular professor’s lab. All students must complete four semesters of proseminar courses, as well as several advanced seminars and statistics classes. Students in human development specialize in one of five concentrations: Aging and Health; Cognitive Development; Developmental Behavioral Neuroscience; Law and Human Development; or Social and Personality Development. Students begin research in their first semester and must complete both a second-year research project and a dissertation. The majority of our graduates obtain positions in academic or research settings.

The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is a one-year, two-semester program that prepares students to design, build, and evaluate the user-facing technologies of the future. The M.P.S. in HCI is based in the field of Information Science. HCI students learn from, and are part of, the broad and deep HCI community at Cornell University.

HCI is the study and practice of designing effective, usable, and satisfying interactive systems. The interdisciplinary field of HCI lies at the intersection of engineering, computer science, behavioral science, and design. Effective HCI requires a mix of technical skills (prototyping, evaluation) and communication skills (explaining and defending one’s work).

Concentration: A.I.D.S., Bacteriology, Cellular Immunology, Clinical Immunology, Comparative Immunology, Genetic and Molecular Immunology, Immunopathology, Parasitology, Tumor Immunology, Virology, Zoo and Wildlife Medicine
Description: The graduate field of Immunology and Infectious Disease (IID) provides outstanding training for students interested in the function of the immune system and the pathogens that subvert it. The IID field brings together faculty from five departments within the College of Veterinary Medicine and two departments at the Ithaca campus of Weill Cornell Medicine to provide a broad and rigorous educational experience that leads to the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in immunology. The goal of the IID field is to provide state-of-the-art training in the concepts and techniques of immunology and host-pathogen interactions. The curriculum is designed to be flexible, so that each student’s course of study can be tailored to their individual needs and interests. Formal coursework is combined with extensive training in research in the laboratory of one of the graduate faculty.

Concentration: Bacteriology, Immunology, Parasitology, Virology, Zoology and Wildlife Conservation
Description: The graduate field of Immunology and Infectious Disease provides interdisciplinary training in the overlapping disciplines of immunology and infection biology, with an emphasis on the basic mechanisms of host-pathogen interactions. The goal of the field is to train the next generation of scientists who will contribute to the understanding and prevention of infectious and inflammatory diseases of animals and humans. The graduate program includes formal course work, journal clubs and research seminars, and original dissertation research. Trainees also develop professional skills such as scientific writing, oral presentation, and networking, which will enable them to succeed in the scientific careers of their choice. Research in the field covers a broad spectrum, including studies of viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens; innate and adaptive immunity; the microbiome; and immune-mediated diseases. State-of-the-art facilities and equipment for cell biology, flow cytometry, genomics, and imaging are available. Students choose their Special Committee chair from among over 30 faculty members who participate in the field. Thesis research is performed in the faculty member’s laboratory.

Concentration: ['Dispute Resolution', 'Human Resources and Organizations', 'International and Comparative Labor', 'Labor Market Policy', 'Labor Relations', 'Organizational Behavior']
Description: The MILR is an interdisciplinary, two-year, professional master’s degree program that provides students with a broad, problem-solving perspective on the world of work and labor. Students have the opportunity to take courses on a variety of subjects within the field of industrial and labor relations, including human resource management, labor relations, dispute resolution, labor economics, organizational behavior, international and comparative labor, and labor law and history. Graduates of the program excel in a variety of careers in business, government, labor unions, and non-profit organizations. Students gain an understanding of how to manage people and organizations; motivate employees; resolve workplace disputes; develop effective negotiating skills; formulate compensation and benefit policies; and analyze labor market trends.

The Master of Professional Studies in Industrial and Labor Relations (M.P.S.) is a one-year, full-time program based in Ithaca, New York, that provides a solid foundation in the various areas of industrial and labor relations. It is designed for practitioners with at least seven to ten years of experience in the various areas of human resources and labor relations. The program prepares students for a variety of positions in business and industry in the United States and abroad. The core courses cover labor relations, human resources, labor economics, organizational behavior, and statistics. Additional elective courses may be taken in these and other areas of the ILR School and elsewhere in the university. A major research paper or project is required.

Concentration: Human Resources and Organizations, International and Comparative Labor, Labor Relations, Labor Economics, and Social Statistics
Description:
The graduate field of Industrial and Labor Relations (ILR) provides a select group of students with an opportunity to pursue advanced study in a variety of specializations within the field. The ILR School offers four graduate degrees: the Master of Industrial and Labor Relations (M.I.L.R.), the Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.), the Master of Science (M.S.), and the Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.).

The M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs are research-focused and designed to train students for academic and research careers. Students in these programs choose to specialize in one of five concentrations: Human Resources and Organizations, International and Comparative Labor, Labor Relations, Labor Economics, and Social Statistics. The M.I.L.R. and M.P.S. degrees are professional master’s degrees, designed to prepare students for careers as practitioners.

Concentration: Human Resource Studies; International and Comparative Labor; Labor Economics; Labor Relations, Law, and History; Organizational Behavior
Description: The graduate field of Industrial and Labor Relations offers M.S. and Ph.D. degrees, with majors in five areas: human resource studies, international and comparative labor, labor economics, labor relations, law and history, and organizational behavior. Students in the M.I.L.R. program pursue a professional master’s degree. The Ph.D. program prepares students for careers as researchers and teachers in universities and research institutions. The M.S. program also is a research-oriented degree, which may be treated as a terminal degree or as the first two years of a doctoral program. The field has about seventy-five faculty members drawn from the School of Industrial and Labor Relations, and the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, and Human Ecology.

The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Information Science is a one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares students for careers as information science professionals. The M.P.S. is offered on the Cornell Ithaca campus and at the Cornell Tech campus in New York City. The Ithaca M.P.S. is a flexible program that allows students to focus on one of many information science sub-fields, including user experience design, data science, and interactive technologies. The Cornell Tech M.P.S. is a more structured program focused on building technology for startups and large companies that provides intensive training in technical systems building and entrepreneurship. More information on the Ithaca-based M.P.S. can be found at the Information Science M.P.S. site. More information on the Cornell Tech M.P.S. can be found at the Cornell Tech site.

Concentration: Connective media, Human-computer interaction, Information policy, Information science of networks, markets, and organizations
Description: The graduate field of information science at Cornell is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the design and use of information systems in a social context. It studies the creation, representation, organization, storage, retrieval, and analysis of information, as well as the impact of information on individuals, groups, organizations, and society. The goal is to produce versatile graduates with the skills to address the myriad challenges of the information age.

Concentration: ['Behavioral science', 'Communication', 'Computational social science', 'Computer-supported cooperative work', 'Crowdsourcing and social computing', 'Digital humanities', 'Human-computer interaction', 'Human-robot interaction', 'Information policy, law, and ethics', 'Network science', 'Social media', 'Sociology', 'Technology and equity', 'User experience design']
Description: The graduate field of Information Science (IS) at Cornell is an interdisciplinary field that addresses the design and use of information systems in a social context. It studies the creation, representation, organization, application, and analysis of information in digital form. The field’s research and teaching are organized into three main hubs that reflect its intellectual core: human computer interaction and design; social and behavioral science; and information, data and society. The hubs integrate methods from computer science, data science, communication, design, law, and sociology. As a discipline, it grew from a confluence of interests among these several academic fields. Students in Information Science are expected to master a core of interdisciplinary material and also to develop a focus in a particular subfield.

Concentration: Controlled Environment Agriculture, Geospatial Applications, Horticulture, Plant Biology, Plant Breeding, Plant Pathology and Plant-Microbe Biology, Soil and Crop Sciences, Public Garden Leadership
Description: The master of professional studies (M.P.S.) is a one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares students for the workplace. The program is ideal for career-changers and recent graduates who want to enter the workforce in an area of agriculture and life sciences. The M.P.S. in Integrative Plant Science program provides students with a graduate-level curriculum focused on the science, management, and policy issues in plant science. Students take courses in the Cornell Graduate School, and may choose from a wide array of options offered throughout the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). The M.P.S. program is distinguished by its capstone project. Instead of a thesis, students complete a project that solves a problem and addresses an issue relevant to the professional world. Projects can be research-based, but are often in the form of internships, curriculum development, extension programs, or in-depth case studies.

Concentration: ['Landscape Architecture', 'Landscape Studies']
Description:
The graduate field of landscape architecture offers two distinct professional master’s degree programs that are nationally accredited by the American Society of Landscape Architects: the first-professional Master of Landscape Architecture (M.L.A. AP) degree and the post-professional Master of Landscape Architecture (M.L.A.) degree. Additionally, the field offers a Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in landscape architecture.

Cornell's Master of Landscape Architecture (M.L.A.) programs prepare students for professional practice and to be leaders in the field. Students explore an array of contemporary and emerging landscape architecture issues, including the relationship between urbanization and ecology, the remaking of post-industrial and post-agricultural landscapes, the challenges of climate change, the role of social and environmental justice, and the importance of ecological democracy. The programs emphasize the art and science of landscape architecture in order to create regenerative landscapes that are not only beautiful, vibrant, and resilient, but also meaningful.

The curriculum is structured in a sequence that equips students with the core knowledge and skills of the discipline while allowing for intellectual and design exploration. Studio is the core of the M.L.A. programs, where students learn to synthesize cultural and ecological systems to create new landscape forms and experiences. Studios are complemented by lectures and seminars that provide in-depth instruction in landscape history and theory, representation, techniques and technologies, and ecological and social processes. The programs engage a range of landscapes, including cities, suburbs, working landscapes, and wildlands.

Cornell's Ithaca campus, with its striking topography, deep gorges, and rich architectural and landscape history, provides an inspirational setting for this work. The expansive Cornell Botanic Gardens, which are located adjacent to the landscape architecture studios, provide an outdoor classroom for learning.
Accredidation: nationally accredited by the American Society of Landscape Architects

Concentration: ['The regular M.P.S. track', 'The Advanced Landscape Studies track']
Description:
The one-year Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Landscape Architecture is an intensive, post-professional degree for those who already have a degree in landscape architecture (B.L.A. or M.L.A.).

The M.P.S. in Landscape Architecture program offers two tracks:

1. The regular M.P.S. track is for individuals who hold an accredited degree in landscape architecture and who wish to specialize in a particular aspect of the field. Potential specializations are unlimited, but often focus on areas such as cultural landscape studies, advanced digital applications, ecological design and restoration, representation, and urbanism.
2. The Advanced Landscape Studies track is for individuals with a landscape architecture degree (or its equivalent) from a foreign institution and a minimum of three years of professional experience who are seeking to augment their knowledge of American practice. This track is not intended to be a path to licensure.

M.P.S. candidates create a highly individualized program of study that is structured by a core design studio, two required landscape architecture seminars, and a capstone project. In addition, candidates take a wide range of elective courses from across the university that are aligned with their particular focus.

The M.P.S. degree is a STEM-designated program in Architectural and Building Sciences/Technology (CIP code 04.0902).

The concurrent degree program in landscape architecture and regional planning provides an opportunity for a student to earn two degrees in a compressed timeframe. Graduates are prepared for professional careers in which design and planning are integrated, for example, in public agencies and private consulting firms that engage in master planning, environmental analysis, site design, urban design, and community development. The program also provides a strong foundation for doctoral studies in either field. The concurrent degree program is coordinated by a joint faculty committee from the two fields. Students must be accepted for admission by both the Graduate Field of Landscape Architecture and the Graduate Field of City and Regional Planning. Students may apply for admission to the concurrent degree program at the time of their initial application to the Graduate School or, for those already enrolled in one of the two fields, at any time during their first two semesters of study.
Accredidation: The M.L.A. degree is accredited by the Landscape Architectural Accreditation Board. The M.R.P. degree is accredited by the Planning Accreditation Board.

Description: The graduate minor in Latin American and Caribbean Studies is a formal academic credential designed for graduate and professional students who have a significant interest in Latin America and the Caribbean but are concentrating in another discipline. The minor provides a structure for interdisciplinary study of the region, and official university recognition of this expertise. The graduate minor is conferred in conjunction with a student’s primary graduate or professional degree. It is administered by the Latin American and Caribbean Studies Program (LACS), part of the Mario Einaudi Center for International Studies. LACS encourages the study of Latin America and the Caribbean across campus and fosters a vibrant community of faculty and students from all disciplines.

Concentration: Business Law and Policy, Constitutional Law, Civil Rights, and Public Law, Criminal Law and Procedure, General Law, Intellectual Property and Technology Law, International and Comparative Law, Litigation, Dispute Resolution, and Legal Process
Description:
The J.S.D. degree is a research doctorate. Holders of this degree are typically teachers of law in their home countries or are in government service. Candidates for this degree are admitted only under special circumstances. Applicants must hold a first degree in law and an LL.M. or a comparable degree. Admission is limited to students who have received their LL.M. degree from Cornell. Admission is highly selective. 

There are no required courses for the J.S.D. program. A J.S.D. student selects an area of concentration and must successfully complete 24 credit hours of courses in that area. The Graduate School requires each J.S.D. candidate to have a Special Committee of three members of the Cornell faculty, one of whom must be from outside the law faculty. The chair of the Special Committee must be a member of the law faculty. The program requires three years of study, the first two of which must be in residence at the Law School. The third year may be spent in absentia, although many students spend the third year in residence.
Accredidation: Cornell Law School is an ABA-approved law school.

Concentration: Cognitive Science, Computational Linguistics
Description:
The graduate field of linguistics at Cornell is a vibrant intellectual community where faculty and graduate students work together on a wide range of topics in theoretical and experimental linguistics. The field’s core strengths are in phonetics/phonology, syntax, and semantics/pragmatics, with additional areas of specialization including historical linguistics, language acquisition, computational linguistics, and psycholinguistics.

Research in the graduate field of linguistics is characterized by a commitment to theoretically-informed empirical investigation based on a diverse range of languages. Many members of the field are also active participants in one or more of the university’s interdisciplinary programs, including Cognitive Science, Computing and Information Science, and area studies programs (e.g., East Asia Program, Southeast Asia Program, South Asia Program).

Concentration: ['Biomaterials', 'Ceramics', 'Composites', 'Electronic materials', 'Metals', 'Polymers', 'Energy production and storage', 'Materials for sustainability', 'Computational materials science']
Description: The graduate field of Materials Science and Engineering (MSE) at Cornell is an interdisciplinary community of faculty, staff, and students from seven departments in the College of Engineering and the College of Arts and Sciences. The field offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs that provide students with a broad education in the fundamental science and engineering of materials. Students also have the opportunity to engage in focused research programs in a number of materials sub-disciplines, including biomaterials, ceramics, composites, electronic materials, metals, and polymers.

Concentration: Biomaterials, Electronic Materials, Energy Production and Storage, Materials for Sustainability, Materials Modeling and Simulation, Nanomaterials, Polymeric Materials, Structural Materials
Description: The graduate field of materials science and engineering at Cornell is a Ph.D.-granting program that attracts students from a wide range of science and engineering disciplines including materials science, chemistry, physics, and mechanical, chemical, electrical and civil engineering. The field offers a flexible, interdisciplinary program, leading to M.S. and Ph.D. degrees that can be tailored to a student’s specific interests. Emphasis is on the generic science of materials that underlies a wide range of engineering applications, from information technology to biotechnology to energy technology. The field also provides a materials science and engineering minor for students outside the field. A diverse and distinguished faculty of more than 40 members offers research opportunities in a broad range of topics. These include: ceramics, complex fluids, composites, electronic materials, metals, and polymers for a wide variety of applications. Students also have access to the world-class characterization and fabrication facilities of the Cornell Center for Materials Research, the Cornell NanoScale Science & Technology Facility, the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source, and the Center for Advanced Computing.

Concentration: ['algebra', 'analysis', 'combinatorics', 'geometry', 'logic', 'number theory', 'probability theory', 'topology']
Description:
The graduate program in mathematics at Cornell is a Ph.D. program. Cornell does not offer a master’s degree in mathematics as a terminal degree.

The mathematics program is organized into eight concentrations, corresponding to the main research areas of the department: algebra, analysis, combinatorics, geometry, logic, number theory, probability theory, and topology. Students may switch concentrations at any time.

The program includes a series of introductory courses, advanced topics courses, and research seminars. It is designed so that a typical student will have an advisor and be working on a thesis problem by the end of the second year.

Almost all students are supported as teaching assistants for four semesters. This includes a stipend, a full tuition fellowship, and health insurance. In later years, most students are supported as research assistants.

Concentration: ['Biomechanics', 'Dynamics, Controls, and Robotics', 'Energy and Sustainability', 'Solid Mechanics and Materials', 'Thermal-Fluid Sciences']
Description: The graduate field of mechanical engineering encompasses the fundamental thermal and fluid sciences, as well as the design, analysis, and manufacture of mechanical systems. Students may focus their studies and research in a variety of areas. The M.S. program is a research-based degree that requires completion of a thesis. Some students enter the M.S. program with the intention of continuing on to a Ph.D. A typical M.S. program requires two years of full-time study.

Concentration: ['Biomechanics', 'Dynamics, Controls, and Robotics', 'Energy and Sustainability', 'Fluid Mechanics', 'Materials Processing', 'Mechanics of Materials', 'Thermal Sciences', 'Transportation']
Description: The graduate field of mechanical engineering offers a broad program of study and research in a variety of areas, including: biomechanics; dynamics, controls, and robotics; energy and sustainability; fluid mechanics; materials processing; mechanics of materials; thermal sciences; and transportation. Research is directed toward a Ph.d. or an M.S. degree. There also is a professional Master of Engineering (M.Eng.) degree program.

Concentration: ['Islamic Studies', 'Medieval and Early Modern Studies']
Description: The graduate field of Medieval Studies offers a Ph.D. degree program that provides students with a thorough grounding in the intellectual and material cultures of medieval Europe as well as in the methods and theories of contemporary medieval scholarship. The program’s flexible structure encourages interdisciplinary work. The field brings together more than 30 faculty members from over a dozen departments in the humanities and social sciences. Core faculty in the field represent a broad geographical, chronological, and methodological range, and their courses cover all periods of medieval history and many vernacular languages and literatures, including Old and Middle English, Old Norse, medieval French, Occitan, medieval German, medieval Italian, medieval Spanish, and medieval Welsh. In addition, graduate students in Medieval Studies have direct access to Cornell’s outstanding collections of medieval manuscripts and rare books, which include the Dante and Petrarch collections, the Witchcraft Collection, the Fiske Icelandic Collection, and the Bodman Collection of Coptic manuscripts.

Concentration: Bacteriology, Environmental and Applied Microbiology, Eukaryotic Microbiology, Immunology and Microbial Pathogenesis, Microbial Biochemistry and Physiology, Microbial Genetics and Genomics, Virology
Description:
The graduate field of microbiology at Cornell has a long and distinguished history. It is one of the few fields in the country that spans the study of the three domains of life: bacteria, archaea, and eukarya. More than 60 faculty from 16 departments in six colleges across the Ithaca campus are members of the graduate field, providing students with a broad choice of research areas and mentors.

Students apply to the field of microbiology and not to a specific faculty member. During the first semester, students attend a series of faculty talks and perform three laboratory rotations, which provide a broad exposure to the research opportunities in the field. At the end of the first semester, students select a major professor and a research area for their dissertation work.
