Research in microbiology at Cornell uses state-of-the-art approaches to study fundamental problems in bacteriology, eukaryotic microbiology, immunology and microbial pathogenesis, microbial biochemistry and physiology, microbial genetics and genomics, virology, and environmental microbiology. Modern biology has been revolutionized by genomic science, and research in microbiology has moved from the study of single genes or proteins to a systems biology approach, in which the goal is to understand how all the parts work together to make the whole. At Cornell, students in microbiology are immersed in a rich and supportive research and training environment where they can apply genomic, proteomic, and bioinformatic approaches to the study of microorganisms. This systems approach is not restricted to any one group of microorganisms, but instead is a unifying theme that ties together the diverse research interests of the faculty in the field.

Concentration: ['Environmental and Applied Microbiology', 'Eukaryotic Microbiology', 'Prokaryotic Microbiology', 'Microbial Biochemistry, Physiology and Diversity', 'Microbial Genetics and Molecular Biology', 'Microbial Pathogenesis', 'Virology']
Description: The graduate field of microbiology at Cornell has a long and distinguished history. Members of the field represent a broad range of interests within the discipline, from the fundamental aspects of microbial physiology, genetics, and development to the applied aspects of bioremediation, plant pathology, and industrial biotechnology. Faculty are drawn from several departments, primarily the Department of Microbiology, which resides in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences. Faculty are also drawn from the College of Engineering and the College of Veterinary Medicine.

Concentration: ['Developmental Physiology', 'Endocrinology', 'Molecular and Cell Physiology', 'Neurophysiology', 'Nutritional Physiology', 'Systems and Integrative Physiology']
Description: The graduate field of molecular and integrative physiology offers programs of study leading to the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees. The field has an exceptionally broad range of research interests, and areas of focus are loosely grouped into the following categories: endocrinology; systems and integrative physiology; cell, molecular, and developmental physiology; and neurophysiology. Students may work with faculty in the College of Veterinary Medicine, the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Arts and Sciences, and the College of Engineering. Prospective students apply for admission to the field as a whole and select a special committee chair and research area during the first semester.

Concentration: Cellular and Molecular Physiology, Endocrinology and Reproductive Physiology, Systems Physiology
Description:
The graduate field of molecular and integrative physiology offers a broad interdisciplinary program of study leading to the Ph.D. degree. The faculty is drawn from eight departments in the College of Veterinary Medicine, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, College of Arts and Sciences, and College of Engineering.

Research training is offered in the general areas of cellular and molecular physiology, endocrinology and reproductive physiology, and systemic physiology. The field is organized to provide maximum flexibility in the design of student programs. The selection of a special committee is of paramount importance. Normally this committee consists of the thesis adviser and two or three other faculty members who represent the student’s major and minor areas of interest. Course work is determined by the student and their special committee and is tailored to the individual’s background, interests, and needs.

All students are required to participate in a teaching program to gain experience. Seminars on selected topics and research in progress are held regularly. Opportunities are available for training in molecular biology and functional genomics, quantitative biology, bioengineering, and biomedical sciences through a variety of NIH- and USDA-sponsored interdepartmental training grants. Students are expected to complete the program in four to five years.

Concentration: Composition
Description: The graduate field of music at Cornell offers two distinct doctoral programs: a Ph.D. in musicology and a D.M.A. in composition. The Ph.D. program is designed for students who wish to pursue a career in teaching and scholarship. The D.M.A. program is intended for composers who wish to teach in a college, university or conservatory. The M.F.A. in composition is no longer offered for admission.

Concentration: Composition
Description: The graduate field of music offers three degree programs: the Ph.D. in musicology, the Doctor of Musical Arts (D.M.A.) in composition, and the Master of Fine Arts (M.F.A.) in composition. These programs provide a broad foundation in music history, theory, and performance practices. Ph.D. students specialize in historical musicology or in ethnomusicology. D.M.A. and M.F.A. students specialize in composition.

Concentration: ['historical musicology', 'ethnomusicology', 'composition']
Description: The graduate field of music offers three concentrations: historical musicology, ethnomusicology, and composition. The Ph.D. in musicology (historical musicology and ethnomusicology) prepares students for careers in scholarship and teaching at the university level. The D.M.A. in composition provides composers with the opportunity to develop their creative and intellectual potential to the fullest. The program is flexible and accommodates students with a wide range of interests. Students benefit from an exceptionally strong music faculty and the extensive resources of one of the world’s great research universities, including an outstanding music library. They are encouraged to pursue in-depth studies in a variety of areas of music scholarship and performance, as well as opportunities for collaborative and interdisciplinary research projects.

Concentration: ['Environmental and Sustainability Communication', 'Environmental and Sustainability Management', 'Fisheries and Aquatic Science', 'Forest Resources Management', 'Sustainable Landscapes', 'Sustainable Water Management', 'Individually-designed concentration']
Description: The Master of Professional Studies (MPS) in Natural Resources and the Environment is an interdisciplinary, one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares students for careers in environmental management and sustainability. Students in our program are recent graduates, returned Peace Corps volunteers and career professionals from non-profit organizations, government agencies and the private sector. Through coursework, a capstone project and professional development opportunities, students acquire the knowledge, skills and networks to be leaders in the environmental field.

Concentration: ['Applied ecology', 'Community-based resource management', 'Ecosystem science and management', 'Environmental governance', 'Environmental and resource economics', 'Quantitative ecology', 'Risk analysis and management']
Description: The graduate field of natural resources and the environment addresses the coupled social-ecological dimensions of natural resource management. Students in our graduate field engage with faculty from many disciplines to learn about the biological, physical, and social aspects of natural resource use and management. Our M.S. and Ph.D. students pursue research degrees that require a final thesis or dissertation. Students have access to state-of-the-art facilities and outstanding field stations that include the Arnot Teaching and Research Forest, the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest, the Cornell Biological Field Station at Shackelton Point, and the Shoals Marine Laboratory. Most students conduct their work in close collaboration with the New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, the Cornell Center for a Sustainable Future, the Cornell Institute for Climate Smart Solutions, the Cornell Water Resources Institute, the Human Dimensions Research Unit, the Center for Conservation Social Sciences, or the Center for the Environment. Students often work closely on applied problems with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation or other state and federal agencies and non-governmental conservation organizations.

Concentration: ['Environment and Society', 'Forest Resources', 'Human Dimensions of Natural Resource Management', 'Quantitative and Spatial Ecology', 'Risk Analysis and Management', 'Water Resources', 'Wildlife Ecology and Management']
Description: The graduate field of natural resources and the environment addresses the coupled-social ecological dimensions of landscapes and watersheds. Research problems are complex and require interdisciplinary teams of social and biophysical scientists. Faculty in our graduate field have expertise across the social and ecological sciences. Students learn to frame, analyze, and address research questions that advance both theory and the sustainable management of natural resources.

Concentration: Ancient Near Eastern studies (including the Hebrew Bible), Arabic and Islamic studies, Egyptology
Description: The graduate program in Near Eastern studies provides students with the opportunity to develop an advanced, interdisciplinary understanding of the languages, literatures, history, and archaeology of the Near East. The field offers Ph.D. and terminal M.A. degree programs. Students choose to specialize in one of the following areas: Ancient Near Eastern studies (including the Hebrew Bible), Arabic and Islamic studies, or Egyptology. Within each area, students formulate a course of study and research in consultation with their Special Committee that can encompass the fields of archaeology, art history, history, languages, and literatures. Students also participate in a cross-disciplinary seminar during the first year of the program that serves as an introduction to current research and methodologies in the field. Students can obtain a minor in any of the areas of specialization within the field, or in other related fields.

The graduate field of neurobiology and behavior is a group of over 50 faculty members from more than a dozen different departments in five colleges at Cornell. The field is organized to bring together faculty and students with a common interest in neurobiology and behavior. A major goal of the field is to promote a multi-disciplinary approach to research. An equally important goal is to provide a cohesive graduate training environment that enables students to mature into first-rate scientists and colleagues, fully prepared for a career in research and teaching in either an academic or industrial environment. Students design their own curriculum in consultation with their Special Committee, in order to gain a broad background in neurobiology and behavior as well as the specialized knowledge required for their thesis research. Students are encouraged to develop a program of study that crosses traditional disciplinary boundaries. Students participate in a number of seminars and journal clubs each semester.

Concentration: Animal Behavior, Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience, Computational Neuroscience, Neuroethology, Systems Neuroscience
Description: The graduate field of neurobiology and behavior is one of the premier programs in the world for training in neuroscience. Our more than 100 faculty members, from more than 25 departments in 7 colleges, conduct research on all aspects of the nervous system, from molecules to behavior, in a wide range of animal species. Research is aimed at understanding the fundamental mechanisms of nervous system function and the neural basis of behavior.

Concentration: ['Molecular nutrition', 'Human nutrition', 'Community nutrition', 'International nutrition']
Description:
The graduate field of nutritional sciences has a long and respected history at Cornell. The field is composed of over 40 faculty members from 13 academic departments with interests spanning the broad area of nutrition. The field offers Ph.D. and M.S. degrees with specializations in molecular nutrition, human nutrition, community nutrition, and international nutrition. M.S. students typically specialize in one of these areas. Students in the M.S. program are frequently self-funded or are supported through a faculty member's research grant. M.S. students must successfully complete a research project and thesis under the direction of their Special Committee.

Cornell’s Didactic Program in Dietetics (DPD) and the Dietetic Internship (DI) are both accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND). The combined DPD/DI programs and the M.S. degree provide students with the opportunity to become registered dietitian/nutritionists (RDN). Cornell participates in the DI match for M.S. applicants who have a verification statement from an ACEND-accredited DPD program. Applicants who have not completed DPD requirements but hold a bachelor’s degree from an accredited college or university may meet the DPD requirements at Cornell as part of their M.S. degree program, then complete our Dietetic Internship.

Concentration: ['Dietetics', 'Global food systems', 'Human nutrition intervention', 'Molecular nutrition', 'Obesity and the metabolic syndrome', 'Paradox of the ponderal plague']
Description: The graduate field of nutritional sciences has a distinguished history of leadership in research and education. Our faculty are engaged in a wide range of basic and applied research, using approaches that range from the molecular to the societal. Students conduct research on humans, animals, and cells to create new knowledge about health, disease, and the role of nutrition and diet. Our doctoral program trains students to become independent investigators in a wide variety of settings. Students learn how to identify important research questions and how to design, conduct, and interpret experiments to answer those questions. Upon completion of the Ph.D. program, students are well qualified to secure postdoctoral or faculty positions at research universities, research positions in government agencies or industry, or positions in public health or clinical nutrition.

ProgramName: (M.S.) in Operations Research and Information Engineering
Concentration: Applied Operations Research, Data Analytics, Financial Engineering, Information Technology, Manufacturing, Strategic Operations, Systems Engineering, M.S. in ORIE ( Ithaca), M.S. in ORIE ( Cornell Tech)
Description:
The graduate field of ORIE at Cornell offers a Ph.D. degree, two research-oriented M.S. degrees, and a professional M.Eng. degree.

The M.S. degrees are intended primarily for students who are interested in a research-oriented degree that might lead on to a Ph.D. degree. The Ph.D. program is for students who plan a career in research and teaching. The M.Eng. program emphasizes professional practice and is intended for students who plan to work in industry. The graduate field of ORIE includes faculty from the School of ORIE, the Department of Mathematics, the Department of Computer Science, the Johnson Graduate School of Management, and the Cornell Tech campus in New York City. Cornell offers an unparalleled combination of breadth and depth of expertise in all of the core methodological areas of the field.

ProgramName: (Ph.D.) in Operations Research and Information Engineering
Concentration: ['Applied Probability and Statistics', 'Data Science', 'Financial Engineering', 'Information Technology', 'Manufacturing', 'Mathematical Programming', 'Semester in Strategic Operations']
Description:
The graduate field of Operations Research and Information Engineering (ORIE) offers a Ph.D. program for students who are interested in pursuing an academic or research career in the field.

The ORIE Ph.D. program prepares students for a variety of careers in academia and industry. Recent graduates have been placed in ORIE, Industrial Engineering, and Business programs at leading universities, as well as in industrial research labs, the financial services industry, and consulting firms.

Students admitted to the ORIE Ph.D. program usually have an undergraduate or master’s degree in engineering, mathematics, computer science, or a physical science. We admit a small, select group of students each year. Financial assistance is available in the form of fellowships, research assistantships, and teaching assistantships. All Ph.D. students are typically fully funded for five years.

Applicants interested in the M.Eng. degree should apply to the field of Systems Engineering.

The graduate field of Performing and Media Arts (PMA) offers a Ph.D. in performance and media studies, a two-year M.F.A. in creative visual media (e.g. film, video, and new media art) or design (scenic, lighting, and costume), and a two-year M.A. in performance and media studies. A Ph.D./M.A. is not offered in creative writing or dance.

The Ph.D. in performance and media studies offers a theoretical and historical framework for studying a range of performance and media forms, with courses in theatre and performance theory, cinema and media studies, theatre history and historiography, and performance as research. Students work with an international faculty who specialize in a wide range of fields, including: film and media studies, theatre history, performance studies, sound studies, dance and movement practices, acting and directing, design, new media, and Asian performance. Ph.D. students have an opportunity to participate in the artistic life of the department and may incorporate performance practice as a component of their research. They may also take courses with graduate faculty in related fields, including but not limited to: Anthropology, Art, Art History, Asian Studies, Classics, Comparative Literature, English, German Studies, Government, Music, and Romance Studies. Cornell offers a number of graduate minors that PMA students may also pursue including: Film and Video Studies, Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, and Visual Studies.

Concentration: ['Molecular and Integrative Pharmacology', 'Systems and Computational Pharmacology', 'Pharmacology Education']
Description: The graduate Field of Pharmacology at Cornell University is an inter-college, inter-departmental, and multi-campus program administered by the Graduate School. The research interests of the Field’s more than 50 faculty members are diverse and represent the entire spectrum of modern pharmacological sciences. Students in the Field of Pharmacology choose from one of three concentrations: Molecular and Integrative Pharmacology; Systems and Computational Pharmacology; or Pharmacology Education. Training emphasizes a combination of didactic course work, seminars and journal clubs, and original laboratory research. The research project is the most important element of the training, and students select a research preceptor and a project during their first year of study.

Concentration: Systems, Molecular, and Cellular Pharmacology
Description: The graduate field of pharmacology provides research training focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms of drug action and the basis of disease. As such, it is an integrative discipline that bridges biomedical and clinical sciences. Research in the field of pharmacology uses all the tools of modern biology, from molecular and cellular to organismal, to investigate how chemical agents, both natural and synthetic, affect biological systems. These studies can provide the basis for the rational design of new therapies and the safer, more effective use of existing medicines.

Concentration: ['Aesthetics', 'Ancient Philosophy', 'Epistemology', 'Ethics and Political Philosophy', 'History of Philosophy', 'Logic', 'Metaphysics', 'Philosophy of Language', 'Philosophy of Mind', 'Philosophy of Science', 'Asian Philosophy']
Description: The graduate program in philosophy is designed to provide the training and the opportunity to do original research in philosophy. It leads to the Ph.D. degree; the M.A. is a degree in course. Admission is to the Ph.D. program. A central part of the program is a series of nine graduate seminars the student is required to take in the first three years of study. In addition to general seminars, in which a variety of topics may be discussed, the offerings are in the main areas of philosophy: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, and history of philosophy. Seminars are also offered in aesthetics, political philosophy, philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, philosophy of science, and philosophy of religion. Graduate students are encouraged to take advantage of the many courses of instruction and other intellectual activities in the department and the University that are relevant to their interests.

ProgramName: (M.S.) in Plant Pathology and Plant-Microbe Biology
(Ph.D.) in Plant Pathology and Plant-Microbe Biology
Bachelor of Arts in Africana Studies
Requirements: Application requirements for this undergraduate program are managed centrally by the college. For the College of Arts & Sciences, first-year applicants must submit the Common Application, a School Report, a Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, a Midyear Report, official transcripts, and the Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement. An interview is not required or offered.
Concentration: African, African American, or Caribbean studies
Description: The Africana Studies major is a liberal arts course of study that is at once a specific area of concentration and a body of knowledge that serves as a foundation for a variety of professions and fields of graduate study. Africana Studies majors have established careers in law, medicine, business, education, communications, politics, and the arts. Students are able to choose one of three concentrations: African, African American, or Caribbean studies.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Agricultural Sciences
Requirements: To apply as a first-year applicant, you will need to submit the following: Common Application (CA), School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, Official Transcript, and the Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement (CA).
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Fees: New York State Resident: $45,842/Year; Out-of-State Resident: $68,380/Year
Concentration: ['Animal Science', 'Business Management and Marketing', 'Crop Production and Management', 'Education and Society', 'Sustainable Agriculture']
Description: The Agricultural Sciences major provides students with a broad-based foundation in the agricultural sciences, which will prepare them for a wide range of careers in production agriculture, as well as in allied industries. The major is designed to provide students with the flexibility to tailor their course of study to meet their individual interests, as well as to develop a deep and rich understanding of the science and art of agriculture. Students in the Agricultural Sciences major work closely with an academic advisor to design a program of study that helps them achieve their academic and professional goals. The curriculum is designed to prepare students for the challenges and opportunities in the agricultural sciences in the 21st century. Students interested in studying agriculture education should also select this major. Students completing the Agricultural Sciences major may also choose to earn a New York State provisional teaching certificate in agricultural education for grades K-12.
ScholarshipType: Need-based grants, scholarships, loans, student employment

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in American Studies
Requirements: First-year applicants to the College of Arts & Sciences must submit the Common Application, Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, Two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, and Official transcript(s).
Description: The American Studies Program provides a multidisciplinary approach to the study of the United States and the Americas. The program is committed to the study of race, ethnicity, and indigeneity; class, gender, and sexuality; and empire, colonialism, and globalization. American Studies is a field that brings a variety of disciplinary and theoretical perspectives to bear on the study of the multiple histories, cultures, and political economies of the Americas. The program encourages students to think capaciously and critically about what constitutes “America” as a historical, political, and cultural idea and how that idea has been contested and reimagined across time and from different social positions and locations. Drawing on the resources of the various departments in the humanities and social sciences, the program offers a wide range of courses. Students are required to take a two-course sequence, which serves as the intellectual core of the major. These courses are distinguished by their focus on theory and method and by their interdisciplinary approach. Majors work with an advisor to craft a coherent plan of study by selecting a concentration of at least six courses organized around a theme, a historical period, or an approach. The program encourages students to consider a semester in the Cornell in Washington Program. Courses in American Studies can be used to satisfy a number of college distribution requirements. For further information, students should consult the American Studies Program website or the American Studies Director of Undergraduate Studies.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Animal Science
Requirements: To apply as a first-year applicant, you will need to submit: Common Application; Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement (CALS), which includes a program-specific essay; Official secondary/high school transcript(s); Counselor recommendation; Two teacher evaluations; and Midyear Report. Cornell has a test-optional policy for SAT/ACT scores. Recommended high school coursework includes 4 units of English, 4 units of mathematics (including calculus), 3 units of science (biology, chemistry, and physics recommended), and 3 years of one foreign language.
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Animal Nutrition', 'Animal Physiology and Growth', 'Animal Management and Welfare', 'Dairy Management', 'Equine Science', 'Pre-veterinary Medicine', 'Individualized Concentration']
Description: The Animal Science curriculum provides a broad background in the biological and physical sciences and their application to the multi-faceted field of animal science. The curriculum provides a strong base for students with a wide variety of career interests, including veterinary medicine, livestock production, agribusiness, companion and service animal management, biomedical science, and conservation of endangered species. Qualified students have opportunities to participate in research projects with faculty members and may also compete for fellowships to conduct research during the summer.

Anthropology is the study of human diversity around the world. Anthropologists study cross-cultural differences and similarities in social institutions, cultural beliefs, and communicative practices. We examine the biological and biocultural origins of our species and the material remains of past societies. In our teaching and research we connect the humanities, the social sciences and the natural sciences. The anthropology major at Cornell provides students with a broad understanding of the discipline’s three subfields: sociocultural anthropology, anthropological archaeology, and biological anthropology. Sociocultural anthropologists explore the diversity of contemporary cultures and social institutions, from global corporations to religious movements. Anthropological archaeologists analyze the material remains of past societies to understand the development of social and cultural life over long periods of time. Biological anthropologists study the evolutionary history and biological variation of our species by analyzing fossils, primate relatives, and the human genome. Courses in the major address a wide range of topics, including: political and legal anthropology; medical anthropology; environmental anthropology; the anthropology of food and cuisine; human-animal relations; religion and ritual; race, gender and sexuality; and the ethnography and archaeology of various world regions (e.g., the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific). The major prepares students for graduate careers in anthropology and a variety of other fields, including law, medicine, public health, development, conservation, and education.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Applied Economics and Management
Department: Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management
Concentration: ['Accounting', 'Agribusiness Management', 'Applied Economics', 'Business Analytics', 'Entrepreneurship', 'Environmental, Energy, and Resource Economics', 'Finance', 'Food Industry Management', 'International Trade and Development', 'Marketing', 'Strategy']
Description: The undergraduate program in Applied Economics and Management (AEM) is a four-year course of study for students who want to have a positive impact on the world around them by applying a strong foundation in economics and management to a variety of complex challenges. It has an applied focus, which means students not only become strong analytical thinkers, they also learn how to use those skills to solve real-world problems. The AEM major offers a distinct advantage because it is based in both the AACSB-accredited Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management and the highly-esteemed College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). This unique combination provides students with a strong foundation in economics and business, grounded in a real-world, problem-solving context. Through this approach, students learn to critically analyze complex situations and to implement effective, practical solutions.
Accredidation: The Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management is accredited by the Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business (AACSB).

Concentration: Art and Architecture, Material Culture Studies, Old World Archaeology, New World Archaeology, Skeletal Biology
Description: The major in Archaeology is an interdisciplinary program that includes faculty from a variety of departments, including: Anthropology, Classics, History of Art, Landscape Architecture, and Near Eastern Studies. The major is administered by the Cornell Institute of Archaeology and Material Studies (CIAMS). Archaeology is the study of the past through material remains. Archaeologists study all of the past, from the origins of humankind to the present day. Archaeology students at Cornell may specialize in a geographic region (e.g., North America, Mesoamerica, South America, Europe, the Mediterranean, the Near East, Africa) and a time period, from prehistory to the recent past. They learn the methods and theories of archaeology, and about the modern practice of archaeology as a profession.

Requirements: All first-year applicants must submit the Common Application (CA), Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, and an official transcript. For the Bachelor of Architecture (B.Arch.) program, applicants are also required to submit a portfolio and complete an interview. The portfolio should consist of 15-20 images showcasing freehand drawings and work in other media. Required high school coursework includes: 4 units of English, 3 units of mathematics (including pre-calculus), 3 units of science (including physics), and 3 units of a foreign language. One unit of physics and four units of math (including calculus) are recommended.
Department: College of Architecture, Art, and Planning
Description: The Bachelor of Architecture (B.Arch.) is a five-year professional degree program that is structured to integrate a broad liberal arts education with a solid intellectual base in architecture. The curriculum is composed of a balanced sequence of courses in the areas of design, history-theory, technology, representation, and electives. At its core is the design studio, a place for inquiry, critical thinking, and experimentation. Design studios are complemented and supported by a robust curriculum of required and elective courses that provide a broad and deep understanding of the history and theory of architecture, technology and tectonics, landscape and urbanism, as well as representation and visual culture. The B.Arch. curriculum includes a significant number of free electives that enables students to pursue a minor or a concentration, to study abroad, or simply to explore the breadth of intellectual and cultural resources available at Cornell.
Accredidation: The B.Arch. degree is accredited by the National Architectural Accrediting Board (NAAB), and the program is ranked as one of the top architecture programs in the United States.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Asian Studies
Requirements: Required application materials for first-year applicants include the Common Application (CA), School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement (CA), an $80 application fee or fee waiver, and official transcript(s).
Concentration: ['China and Asia-Pacific Studies', 'South Asia Studies', 'Southeast Asia Studies']
Description: The Department of Asian Studies offers a major in Asian Studies to students enrolled in the College of Arts and Sciences. The major is designed to develop a student’s command of an Asian language and to provide a broad-based understanding of a geographical or cultural area within Asia. The major can be pursued through two options: the general Asian Studies major or the more specialized concentration in China and Asia-Pacific Studies. The China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CAPS) concentration has its own separate admission and curricular requirements.

The Astronomy major is intended to provide a firm foundation in astronomy and astrophysics for students interested in a career in the field. The major requires a strong background in physics and mathematics. A research course (ASTRO 4940), an advanced course, a senior seminar (ASTRO 4490), and one additional advanced course are required. Majors are expected to attend the weekly undergraduate research and pizza seminar (ASTRO 4499) and the departmental colloquia (ASTRO 6990/ASTRO 7990). The major requirements are listed here, as well as on the departmental webpage.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Atmospheric Science
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Fees: $46,264/Year for New York state residents; $68,380/Year for non-New York state residents.
Concentration: ['Climate Science Specialization', 'Environmental Geosciences Specialization', 'Financial Risk Management Specialization', 'Meteorology Specialization', 'Ocean Sciences Specialization']
Description:
The undergraduate program in Atmospheric Science provides students with a strong foundation in the fundamentals of meteorology and the option for in-depth study in a variety of other areas, including climate science, financial risk management, and environmental science. The major has a strong science base of physics and math as a foundation for the required courses in atmospheric dynamics, thermodynamics, and weather analysis and forecasting. In addition to the core atmospheric science courses, students are required to complete a specialization to provide more depth in their area of interest. Research opportunities are available with faculty in the department, and students may elect to write an honors thesis during their senior year. All majors have the opportunity to participate in the Cornell Chapter of the American Meteorological Society, the Cornell Weather forecast team, and the Northeast Regional Climate Center, all of which are housed in the department.

For students interested in a career in operational meteorology, this major satisfies the requirements of the American Meteorological Society for the Certified Broadcast Meteorologist designation and of the federal government for employment as a meteorologist. Opportunities for atmospheric science graduates include careers in weather forecasting, environmental consulting, the air quality sector, the energy and insurance industries, and a wide array of other private companies and government agencies. Many graduates also go on to graduate school to pursue more advanced studies and a career in research. Students majoring in atmospheric science can also complete a second major or a minor in a variety of other fields. Common choices include a second major in the College of Engineering or minors in business, climate change, computer science, and a senior thesis.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Biological Engineering
Department: College of Engineering and College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Fees: College of Engineering: $68,380/Year. College of Agriculture and Life Sciences: $46,444/Year for NYS residents, $68,380/Year for out-of-state residents (2024-2025 rates).
Concentration: ['Biomedical Engineering', 'Biomechanics and Mechanobiology', 'Bioinstrumentation and Bioimaging', 'Drug Delivery and Nanomedicine', 'Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine', 'Synthetic and Systems Biology', 'Biomaterials', 'Computational Biology', 'Sustainability for Food, Energy, and Water Systems', 'Ecological Engineering', 'Soil and Water Engineering', 'Digital Agriculture']
Description: Biological engineering is at the interface of engineering and biology. It is a field that is based on the application of engineering principles to biological systems to solve problems in a wide variety of fields, from medicine to the environment. The Biological Engineering (B.S.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org, under the General Criteria and the Program Criteria for Biological and Similarly Named Engineering Programs. The biological engineering (BE) major is a demanding, multidisciplinary program for students who are strong in the physical sciences and who also have a keen interest in biology. The program provides a strong foundation in the engineering sciences, including thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, and transport phenomena. It also provides a strong foundation in basic biological sciences, including biochemistry, molecular biology, and microbiology. Building upon this, students learn to quantitatively analyze biological systems and to design and build instruments and processes to solve a wide array of societal problems. Biological engineering graduates are well prepared for careers in a wide array of fields, including medicine, biomedical engineering, environmental engineering, and biotechnology. Our graduates have also found employment in biotechnology, pharmaceutical, and food industries, as well as in environmental and biomedical consulting firms.
Accredidation: The Biological Engineering (B.S.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org, under the General Criteria and the Program Criteria for Biological and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Biological Sciences
Requirements:
As this is an undergraduate program, applicants must submit the Common Application, Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement, a School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, a Midyear Report, an official high school transcript, and an $80 application fee or fee waiver.

Since the Biological Sciences (BA) major is offered through two different colleges, applicants must meet the high school coursework requirements for the college they are applying to:

1. College of Arts & Sciences: 4 units of English, 4 units of mathematics (including calculus), 3 units of science, and 3 units of one foreign language.

2. College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS): 4 units of English, 4 units of Mathematics, and 3 units of Science (Biology, Chemistry, and Physics are recommended). One year of biology and one year of chemistry are required.
Concentration: ['Animal Physiology', 'Biochemistry', 'Computational Biology', 'Ecology and Evolutionary Biology', 'General Biology', 'Genetics, Genomics and Development', 'Human Nutrition', 'Insect Biology', 'Microbiology', 'Molecular and Cell Biology', 'Neurobiology and Behavior', 'Plant Biology', 'Systematics and Biotic Diversity']
Description: The biological sciences major offers a unified curriculum for undergraduates in the College of Arts and Sciences and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. The major is administered by the Office of Undergraduate Biology (OUB). The OUB, located in 216 Stimson Hall, is the primary source of information and advising for all students interested in the major. Students in each college are guided by a college-level faculty advisor in their respective college. The biological sciences major is one of the largest majors on campus. The faculty who participate in the major are from many Cornell colleges and departments. Students are exposed to the excitement and challenge of modern biological sciences while they pursue a curriculum that is tailored to their specific interests.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Biological Sciences
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences; College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: ['Animal Physiology', 'Biochemistry', 'Computational Biology', 'Ecology and Evolutionary Biology', 'General Biology', 'Genetics, Genomics and Development', 'Human Nutrition', 'Insect Biology', 'Microbiology', 'Molecular and Cell Biology', 'Neurobiology and Behavior', 'Plant Biology', 'Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems', 'Systematics and Biotic Diversity']
Description: The biological sciences major is a new major jointly offered by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences. The major in biological sciences provides a unified curriculum for undergraduate students in the life sciences at Cornell. It is based on the conviction that a common core of knowledge and a common set of approaches are required for all life scientists. To this end, the major offers a curriculum that is both broad and deep, that can be flexibly tailored to a student’s interests, and provides an excellent preparation for graduate study, professional schools (in medicine, dentistry, and veterinary medicine), and for careers in many areas of biology. A key feature of the major is the requirement that students participate in an in-depth learning experience outside of the traditional classroom, including undergraduate research, study abroad, or an internship. The biological sciences major provides a rigorous and comprehensive education in the life sciences through its breadth requirements and thirteen concentrations.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Biology & Society
Department: College of Arts and Sciences; College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Fees: $43,888/Year (NYS residents in College of Agriculture and Life Sciences); $65,204/Year (Out-of-state residents and students in College of Arts and Sciences)
Concentration: The program requires students to organize their courses into a thematic concentration. Examples of thematic concentrations include: Environment, Health and disease, Law, policy, and ethics, Food, agriculture, and society.
Description:
The Biology & Society major is intended for students who wish to combine the study of biology with exposure to perspectives from the social sciences and humanities on the social, political and ethical aspects of modern biology. The major is interdisciplinary and intercollegiate. It is offered by the Department of Science & Technology Studies in the College of Arts and Sciences and in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. The major is suitable for students who plan to enter careers in which an understanding of the biological sciences and of the social and ethical issues that they raise is of central importance, such as law, medicine, public health, public policy, business, and education.

Students in the Biology & Society major take courses in the biological sciences, as well as core and elective courses in the social sciences and humanities that examine the social, ethical, and policy dimensions of the life sciences. The major is designed to provide a broad understanding of biology, with the precise selection of biology courses tailored to the student’s interests.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Biology & Society
Department: College of Arts and Sciences and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: The Biology & Society major is intended for students who wish to combine the study of biology with exposure to perspectives from the social sciences and humanities. The major is interdisciplinary and is sponsored by the departments of Biological Sciences and Science & Technology Studies. The Biology & Society major is designed for students with a strong interest in the life sciences who also wish to acquire a rich understanding of the social, ethical, and policy dimensions of modern biology. Students in the major will come to appreciate the nature of scientific knowledge and the ways in which science and society are interwoven. Many of the most critical issues of our time—food and population, biotechnology, health and disease, and the environment—are at the intersection of biology and society. The major is thus designed to provide students with the skills and perspectives to systematically confront these and other issues. Graduates have gone on to careers and graduate study in a wide range of fields, such as medicine, law, public health, public policy, environmental studies, and academia.
ScholarshipType: Need-based grants and scholarships, ROTC scholarships

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Biomedical Engineering
Concentration: ['Biomaterials and Drug Delivery (BMDD)', 'Biomedical Imaging and Instrumentation (BMII)', 'Molecular and Cellular Engineering (MCE)', 'Biomechanics and Mechanobiology (BMMB)']
Description: Biomedical engineering is a rapidly growing field that integrates the engineering sciences with biology and medicine. Biomedical engineers design medical devices, develop new therapies, and create diagnostic tools to improve human health. The undergraduate major in Biomedical Engineering (BME) at Cornell provides a strong foundation in the fundamentals of engineering, as well as the life sciences, and then integrates these to study human health. The BME major is designed to provide breadth and depth, allowing students to pursue a wide range of career paths in industry, research, medicine, and beyond.
Accredidation: The B.S. degree in Biomedical Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Biometry and Statistics
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: Statistical Science, Statistical Genomics
Description: The Biometry and Statistics major provides a strong background in statistical and mathematical sciences, and it prepares students for careers in the theory and application of statistics and data science. The curriculum includes a core of statistics and mathematics courses, and it provides an opportunity to specialize by choosing an optional concentration in either Statistical Science or Statistical Genomics. Students acquire skills in statistical reasoning, data analysis and modeling, and computation. They also learn how to communicate the results of their analyses effectively. Graduates are qualified to pursue advanced degrees or to begin professional careers in a variety of fields.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Chemical Engineering
Description: Chemical engineering is involved in the chemical and physical processing of matter and energy that is the basis for our technological society. It is a broad and versatile discipline in which the chemical engineer may design, develop, or operate a process to produce a desired product. Chemical engineers lead the way in new developments in medicine, advanced materials, energy, and the environment. Students are well prepared for graduate study in chemical engineering or for a variety of other fields such as medicine, law, or business, as well as faculty advisers from the field.
Accredidation: The B.S. in Chemical Engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Chemistry and Chemical Biology
Requirements: Required first-year application materials include: the Common Application (CA), Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement (CA), School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, and official transcript(s). Strong high school preparation for the College of Arts & Sciences curriculum includes: 4 units of English, 4 units of mathematics (including calculus), 3 units of science, and 3 units of a single foreign language.
Description: The Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree in Chemistry and Chemical Biology offers a flexible program for students who want to gain a solid background in chemistry while pursuing other interests. The B.A. degree is not accredited by the American Chemical Society. Students in the B.A. program must satisfy the College of Arts and Sciences distribution requirements. Students may also use the B.A. program as a basis for a double major. The chemistry part of the B.A. degree consists of a streamlined set of core courses plus an advanced course and a lab requirement. The program is described below.
Accredidation: The B.A. degree is not accredited by the American Chemical Society.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in China and Asia-Pacific Studies
Requirements: To apply as a first-year applicant, you are required to submit the Common Application (CA), School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report (when available), Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement (CA), an $80 application fee or fee waiver, and official secondary/high school transcript(s). English Language Proficiency Test scores are required for international applicants who do not meet specific criteria.
Description: The China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CAPS) major, based at Cornell and with a semester in Beijing and a semester in Washington, D.C., provides an opportunity for a select group of students to gain a sophisticated understanding of China and its relationship with the U.S. and the Asia-Pacific region. Students in the major gain a strong proficiency in Mandarin Chinese, take a wide array of courses on China’s history, politics, and society, get direct experience of the country, and develop an intellectual focus in a particular area of study. CAPS majors are part of a small cohort that develops close ties to one another and to faculty members affiliated with the program. The major also provides a structured framework for pursuing a rigorous and interdisciplinary study of China.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering
Requirements: To apply as a first-year student, you must submit the Common Application (CA), a School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, a Midyear Report, the Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement (CA), an official transcript from your high school, and an $80 application fee or fee waiver. Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT) are optional.
Concentration: ['Civil Infrastructure (CI)', 'Environment (ENV)', 'Transportation Systems Engineering (TSE)']
Description: Civil engineering is the professional engineering discipline that deals with the design, construction, and maintenance of the physical and naturally built environment. This includes works such as bridges, roads, canals, dams, and buildings. It is a very broad field, composed of several very different sub-disciplines including: structural engineering, materials science, environmental engineering, water resources engineering, geotechnical engineering, and transportation engineering. At Cornell, these sub-disciplines are grouped into three primary areas: Civil Infrastructure (CI), Environment (ENV), and Transportation Systems Engineering (TSE). Students majoring in civil engineering select one of these three areas for primary concentration and another for a secondary concentration. The B.S. CEE degree is a professional degree that provides a basis for professional registration and practice. Civil engineers serve the public in a variety of ways: as municipal engineers; as consultants to architects and other engineers; as construction managers and contractors; as planners of urban and regional transportation and utility systems; and as managers of large public and private corporations. They may be involved with projects of all sizes and complexities, from the design of a small structure or drainage system to the planning of a regional transportation network or the management of a multinational corporation. The B.S. degree program in Civil Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.
Accredidation: The B.S. degree program in Civil Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

Concentration: Option I: Greek and Latin, Option II: Greek, Option III: Latin
Description: The Classics major is designed to give students a thorough grounding in the fundamentals of Greek and Latin and to develop their skills in reading and interpreting the classical languages in their literary and historical contexts. Students will be expected to master the grammar and syntax of Greek and Latin and to become familiar with the major works of the classical authors. At the same time, because the study of the classical world requires a broad interdisciplinary approach, students are strongly encouraged to take courses in such related fields as ancient history, archaeology, ancient philosophy, and the history of art. The Classics Department offers majors in Classics, Classical Civilization, and Latin, and a minor in Classics.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Cognitive Science
Concentration: Cognition and Perception, Language and Linguistics, Computation and Cognition, Neuroscience and Cognition, Culture and Cognition, Cognitive Science in Context
Description: Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of the mind: what it is, how it works, and how it is implemented. The field includes researchers from psychology, linguistics, computer science, philosophy, neuroscience, and anthropology. Questions cognitive scientists ask include: What is the nature of belief and desire? How are memories stored and retrieved? What is the structure of human language? How do we see and hear? What is consciousness? How do we learn? Can machines be intelligent? What is the role of culture in shaping the mind?

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in College Scholar
Requirements:
The application consists of:
1. The College Scholar Application form (downloadable as a Word doc).
2. A detailed essay of about 1000 words. The essay should include:
    - The genesis and articulation of your proposed program of study
    - An explanation of how your program is both rigorous and coherent
    - A discussion of your long-term goals and how this program will help you attain them
3. A proposed course of study for the remainder of your time at Cornell.
4. A copy of your official Cornell transcript (a PDF from Student Center is fine).
5. A letter of recommendation from your faculty advisor.
6. A second letter of recommendation from a faculty member who has taught you in a class or supervised your research at Cornell.
7. Optional: a résumé.
Description: The College Scholar Program offers a small number of students in the College of Arts and Sciences an opportunity to design their own interdisciplinary majors and courses of study. College Scholars design their majors in consultation with a faculty advisory committee of their own choosing. The Program is not an honors program in the conventional sense; it is an opportunity for students with a particular intellectual passion that cannot be pursued within a single traditional department to create a course of study that is uniquely their own. While each College Scholar’s program of study is unique, all Scholars are expected to pursue a course of study that is both rigorous and coherent. As part of their experience in the program, College Scholars participate in a regular seminar in which they present their own work and learn about the work of their peers. All College Scholars are required to complete a senior project, which is typically a written thesis.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Communication and Social Influence', 'Communication, Environment, Science, and Health', 'Individually designed focus area']
Description: The Communication major provides a liberal arts education that prepares students to be effective communicators. Students develop a comprehensive understanding of communication theory and research. They apply this knowledge to a variety of contexts—interpersonal, intercultural, organizational, political, and mediated—and learn how communication processes create, maintain, and transform individual and societal-level identities, institutions, and relationships. Students in the major select a focus area: Communication and Social Influence; Communication, Environment,Science, and Health; or an individually designed focus area.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Comparative Literature
Description: Comparative Literature is the study of literature and culture across national, linguistic, and disciplinary boundaries. The Department of Comparative Literature at Cornell is one of the oldest and most distinguished in the country. It is renowned for its global and theoretical reach, with faculty specializing in a wide variety of literary traditions and critical approaches. The curriculum is unusually flexible and varied. Students design their own course of study in close consultation with their faculty adviser. Majors are encouraged to spend a semester or a year studying abroad, and often do so.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science
Description: The Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) in computer science is offered by the College of Arts and Sciences. It is intended for students who are interested in the computer science field, but not in the comprehensive and intensive program required for a Bachelor of Science (B.S.). In terms of course requirements, this program is less structured than the B.S. program. The B.A. program gives students more opportunity to define their own interests and to combine the study of computing with a study of some other field. That other field might be a second major (e.g. music, economics), or it might be the application of computing in another field (e.g. computer graphics, computational biology, computational linguistics).

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Computer Science
Department: College of Arts and Sciences, College of Engineering
Concentration: External Specialization, Digital Media, Artificial Intelligence, Foundations, Scientific Computing, Software Engineering, Systems and Networking
Description: The computer science (CS) major gives students a thorough grounding in the fundamentals of computer science and a broad choice of advanced electives. Depending on the college, the CS major will earn either a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree from the College of Engineering or a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree from the College of Arts and Sciences. Both degree programs require a common set of core courses. The College of Engineering B.S. program has an additional set of college requirements, collectively referred to as the Common Curriculum.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Design and Environmental Analysis
Requirements: First-year applicants must submit: the Common Application (CA), a School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, an official transcript, and the Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement (CA). For admission to the College of Human Ecology, recommended high school coursework includes: 4 units of English, 4 units of mathematics (including calculus), and 3 units of science (biology, chemistry, and physics are recommended). Applicants to the Design and Environmental Analysis major are required to complete the DEA Design Challenge as part of their application.
Concentration: ['Design Strategy', 'Sustainable Futures', 'Health and Well-being']
Description: The Department of Design and Environmental Analysis (D+EA) is dedicated to creating innovative, sustainable, and healthy environments through a multidisciplinary approach encompassing design, environmental psychology, ergonomics, and facility strategy and management. Our mission is to advance the field and to create a better world by engaging in research, teaching, and outreach that is both human-centered and systems-oriented. D+EA is a world leader in design research and education focused on how the built environment impacts human health and well-being. D+EA students learn how to think critically and creatively to address complex, real-world problems. They master the knowledge and skills needed for professional careers in which they plan, design, and manage residential and commercial environments.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences
Concentration: ['Atmospheric Science', 'Climate Science', 'Geological Sciences', 'Oceanography']
Description: The bachelor of arts (B.A.) in earth and atmospheric sciences provides a strong background in earth science, with a focus on breadth and a liberal arts education. It has a high degree of flexibility, offering students the opportunity for a broad education in the liberal arts and sciences. The B.A. degree is also appropriate for students planning to enter a profession such as law, business, or medicine, where a general science background is valuable. Students are also well-prepared for graduate study in earth and atmospheric sciences or related fields. Completion of the major requires introductory coursework in physics and chemistry, and proficiency in math through two semesters of calculus. Coursework within earth and atmospheric sciences covers a broad range of topics, including fundamentals in geological sciences, atmospheric sciences, and oceanography. Students select at least four intermediate- to upper-level courses from an extensive list of course options, thereby tailoring their major to their interests.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences
Requirements: General requirements for first-year applicants include the Common Application, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, official transcript, and the Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement. An application fee or fee waiver is also required.
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Atmospheric Science', 'Climate Change', 'Environmental Geosciences', 'Geological Sciences', 'Ocean Sciences', 'Science of Earth Systems']
Description:
The Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences (EAS) is an interdisciplinary department with the common goal of advancing knowledge of Earth’s systems and their interactions, from the Earth’s core to its atmosphere and oceans. Our curriculum focuses on the past, present, and future of our planet, its life, and its climate, providing students with a firm foundation in the fundamentals of Earth science, while also emphasizing a systems approach to the study of the Earth.

The major in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences provides a flexible framework for students with a wide range of interests. All students learn about the fundamental physical, chemical, and biological processes that shape the Earth, including the formation of our planet and the solar system; the causes of earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain-building; the structure and circulation of the atmosphere and oceans; the history of life and climate; and the cycling of elements through the Earth’s interior, oceans, and atmosphere. After completing a set of core courses, students select one of six specialized concentrations described below, which allows them to explore their specific interests in greater depth.

The major is appropriate for students who intend to pursue a graduate degree and a research career in the Earth sciences; for those who wish to work in the fields of environmental consulting or management; for those interested in K-12 science education; or simply for those who want a broad-based liberal arts education in a fascinating field.

Requirements: First-year applicants to the College of Arts & Sciences must submit the Common Application, a School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, a Midyear Report, an official transcript, and the Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement. An $80 application fee or fee waiver is also required. Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT) are optional.
Description: Economics is the study of how people make choices under conditions of scarcity, and the results of those choices for society. The subject includes the study of labor, land, and investment; of money, income, and production; and of taxes and government expenditures. Economists seek to measure well-being, to learn how it may increase over time, and to evaluate the public policies that affect it. As a major, economics is useful for careers in business, government, law and graduate study.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Electrical and Computer Engineering
Concentration: ['Computer Engineering', 'Information Systems', 'Electrical Power Engineering', 'Electronics and Photonics', 'Biomedical Engineering', 'Control Systems', 'Electromagnetics', 'Signal Processing']
Description: The Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) curriculum is a four-year program that provides a broad and strong foundation in ECE fundamentals. These fundamentals include circuits, electronics, computer logic, computer organization, and programming, as well as the underlying mathematics and physics. A rich and diverse set of ECE courses is offered at the upper levels in which students learn about and work on state-of-the-art devices, systems, and technologies.
Accredidation: The B.S. degree in Electrical and Computer Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Engineering Physics
Requirements: All first-year applicants are required to submit the Common Application and the Cornell Writing Supplement. The Cornell Engineering essay, which is part of the supplement, asks applicants to describe their interest in engineering. Additional required documents include a School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations (one from a math teacher and one from a science teacher), a Midyear Report, and an official transcript. Required high school coursework for the College of Engineering includes: 1 unit of calculus, 1 unit of physics, and 1 unit of chemistry. It is recommended that applicants have one unit of computer science.
Description: The Department of Engineering Physics offers a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in Engineering Physics. Engineering physics is the smallest of the engineering majors and is administered by the School of Applied and Engineering Physics. The undergraduate program in Engineering Physics is designed for students who want to build a strong and broad foundation in physics and mathematics and use that knowledge to solve modern technological problems. It is a demanding curriculum, but the rewards are great. Students in Engineering Physics take challenging courses from several different departments in both the College of Engineering and the College of Arts and Sciences. This gives our students a flavor for many different styles of learning and many different approaches to problem solving. Our students gain both a broad education in the fundamentals of physics and an in-depth understanding of engineering analysis and design. The program is flexible enough to allow students to prepare for a wide variety of careers. Our curriculum can be tailored to meet the needs of those students who want to continue their formal education in graduate school as well as those who want to enter industry directly after completing their undergraduate degree. We offer a structured curriculum, a friendly and supportive atmosphere for learning and a close interaction with the faculty. Our small size allows us to follow and respond to the specific needs of our students much more closely than larger departments. The B.S. degree in Engineering Physics is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.
Accredidation: The B.S. degree in Engineering Physics is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.

Requirements: To apply as a first-year applicant, you will need to submit the following: Common Application (CA), Cornell University Questions and Writing Supplement (CA), School Report, Counselor Recommendation, Two Teacher Evaluations, Midyear Report, Official transcript(s), English Language Proficiency Test scores (if applicable), $80 application fee or fee waiver.
Concentration: Creative Writing, English and Theatre Cooperative Program, Honors, Law and Society, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) Studies, Minority, Indigenous, and Third World Studies (MITWS), Visual Studies
Description: The English major at Cornell requires a combination of broad literary-historical coverage and a more specialized focus in a particular area of interest. Students must take at least eleven courses in the Department of English (or cross-listed with English) in addition to the First-Year Writing Seminars. Of these eleven courses, two must be at the 2000-level, and at least six must be at the 3000- or 4000-level. Four of the six upper-level courses must be taken in the Cornell English Department. All courses must be taken for a letter grade, and must receive a grade of C or better. Courses must be at least 3 credits. Advanced Placement credit does not count toward the major. Up to two courses offered by other departments at Cornell may be counted toward the major if they are approved by the student’s major advisor. Up to two of the eleven courses may be taken in creative writing. Courses used to fulfill the major must satisfy the following three specific requirements. (Note that one course may satisfy two requirements.) For details on these requirements, please consult the department’s website at english.cornell.edu.

Requirements: CALS requires the following high school coursework: 4 units of math (including calculus), 4 units of English, 3 units of science (biology, chemistry and physics are recommended). A high school diploma or GED is also required.
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Insect Molecular Biology, Systematics, and Ecology', 'Medical and Veterinary Entomology', 'Ecology and Evolutionary Biology of Insects', 'Toxicology and Pest Management']
Description: Entomology is the study of insects, which are the most abundant group of organisms on earth. The major in entomology is designed for students with a special interest in the study of insects and their relationships with people and the environment. As a professional field, entomology includes the study of insect biology and the application of that knowledge to the benefit of humanity. The curriculum provides a basic background in biological and environmental sciences with a special emphasis on the study of insects. Facilities include modern laboratories, an extensive insect collection, a library, and the Dyce Laboratory for Honey Bee Studies. Graduates are prepared for advanced studies in entomology and other biological sciences as well as for employment in various areas of the life sciences.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Environment and Sustainability
Requirements: All first-year applicants must submit the Common Application, a School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Evaluations, a Midyear Report, official transcript, the Cornell Questions and Writing Supplement, and an application fee or fee waiver.
Concentration: ['Environmental Biology & Applied Ecology Concentration', 'Environmental Economics Concentration', 'Environmental Humanities Concentration', 'Environmental Policy & Governance Concentration', 'Land, Air & Water Resources Concentration', 'Student-Designed Concentration']
Description:
The Environment & Sustainability (E&S) major is a multidisciplinary, undergraduate program co-hosted by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences. The E&S major prepares students to address the significant environmental and sustainability challenges of the 21st Century. Students in the E&S major develop:

1) a fundamental understanding of the earth’s natural systems,

2) an appreciation for the social and economic context of environmental issues, and

3) the quantitative and qualitative skills needed for environmental problem-solving.

E&S majors benefit from the unique strengths and resources of two colleges, including world-class faculty in diverse environmental fields, research opportunities, and career advising networks. All E&S majors take a common set of core courses and then specialize in one of six concentrations to gain depth and focus in a particular area of environment and sustainability studies. The E&S major is administered by a cross-campus Program Board with oversight from both colleges. Students are subject to the graduation requirements of their home college and may enroll in the College of Arts and Sciences or the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Environment and Sustainability
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: ['Environmental Biology and Applied Ecology', 'Environmental and Resource Economics', 'Environmental Humanities', 'Environmental Policy and Governance', 'Land, Air, and Water Resources', 'Sustainable Business and Environmental Management', 'Climate Change', 'Community and Urban Environmental Studies', 'Food, Energy, and Water Resources', 'Indigeneity and Environment', 'Sustainable Agriculture', 'Sustainable Development']
Description: The Environment and Sustainability (E&S) major is for students who want to understand the complex system of social and natural interactions that shape our planet. They learn to evaluate the sustainability of human activities by considering social, economic and environmental impacts. The E&S major leads to a B.S. degree from either the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) or the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S). E&S majors apply to and enroll in one college, and follow the requirements of that college. Within the major, students select a concentration area that offers in-depth study in a particular aspect of environment and sustainability. Students from both colleges are part of one cohort of majors who share a set of core courses and a common experience.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Environmental Engineering
Department: College of Engineering and College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: Environmental engineering is the application of basic principles of science and engineering to improve the natural environment (air, water, and land resources) and to provide healthy water, air, and land for human habitation and for other organisms. Environmental engineers are involved in water and air pollution control, recycling, waste disposal, public health issues, and a knowledge of environmental engineering law. They also address global issues such as unsafe drinking water, climate change, and ozone depletion. Cornell’s undergraduate program is designed to provide a broad understanding of the technical, scientific, and managerial skills necessary for a career in environmental engineering. The curriculum builds on a strong foundation of mathematics, physics, and chemistry. Engineering science courses provide an understanding of fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, and transport phenomena, essential to quantitative description of environmental problems. The program also draws on the strengths of Cornell in biology and the earth sciences. A key element of the major is the design experience, which is incorporated into several courses and which culminates with a senior-year capstone design course. Graduates with a B.S. in environmental engineering can pursue a variety of career paths in industry, government, consulting, and nongovernmental organizations. The program also provides a solid background for students who intend to pursue graduate studies in environmental engineering or related fields, or in a professional field such as law, medicine, or business.
Accredidation: The B.S. degree in Environmental Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Feminist, Gender, & Sexuality Studies
Description: The Program in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies offers students the opportunity to study a wide range of topics concerning gender and sexuality, grounded in the analysis of race, class, and ethnicity. Students will learn to think critically about how sex, gender, and sexuality are constructed and policed, and how they operate in both the past and the present, in the United States and across the globe. Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies courses offer an interdisciplinary perspective from which to analyze the formation of identities, practices, and institutions. Students pursue their own questions in an intellectually rigorous environment and in a supportive community of scholars. Courses in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies may be used to fulfill a number of college distribution requirements. The program offers an undergraduate major and two minors: one in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, and one in Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Studies.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Fiber Science & Apparel Design
Concentration: ['Apparel Design', 'Fashion Design Management', 'Fiber Science']
Description: The undergraduate program in fiber science and apparel design (FSAD) has a strong material and design foundation. The curriculum combines chemistry, physics, and math with design, art history, economics, and marketing. Students develop an understanding of the art of design, the science of fibers and fabrics, and the role of technology and merchandising in the apparel and textile industry. State-of-the-art computer-aided design, materials science and engineering, and textile testing laboratories allow students to have a hands-on learning experience. Students choose one of three options: Apparel Design, Fashion Design Management, or Fiber Science.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Fine Arts in Fine Arts
Department: College of Architecture, Art, and Planning
Description: The bachelor of fine arts (B.F.A.) is a professional degree program that focuses on the development of the student as an artist. Students follow a structured curriculum in the creative and liberal arts and sciences. The program provides an opportunity for students to become disciplined in a particular studio practice while gaining a broad humanistic education.
