Students may choose to concentrate in drawing, painting, photography, print media, sculpture, electronic arts, or any combination thereof. The Department of Art is committed to the notion that the liberal arts and studio arts are intimately connected. The curriculum has been designed to allow a student to take full advantage of the resources of the university. Art majors spend about 60 percent of their time in art courses and the remaining 40 percent in academic subjects. B.F.A. candidates must complete 130 credits; 80 of the 130 credits must be in art courses.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Food Science
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: ['Basic Food Science', 'Food Operations and Management', 'Food Engineering']
Description: Food science is an exciting multidisciplinary field that applies chemistry, microbiology, engineering, and nutrition to the development of new food products and the improvement of food safety, quality, and nutrition. The food science major is an excellent program for students interested in a career in the food industry, government, or academia. All students in the food science major gain a solid background in the basic sciences before taking a core of food science courses. The basic food science concentration provides a strong background for graduate study in food science or a related field. The food operations and management concentration is for students interested in business and the more applied aspects of the food industry. The food engineering concentration provides a strong background for students interested in the engineering aspects of the food industry or in graduate school in food engineering or a related engineering field.
Accredidation: The food science major is approved by the Higher Education Committee of the Institute of Food Technologists (IFT).

Description: The French major at Cornell is designed to give students a thorough grounding in the language and a familiarity with French and Francophone literature and culture. It is an appropriate course of study for students who want to go on to graduate school in French or other disciplines (e.g., comparative literature, art history, history, government, business), for those who want to prepare for careers in which a knowledge of French language and culture is a significant asset (e.g., international law, banking, business, or diplomacy), and for those who wish to combine the study of French with other disciplines (e.g., in a double major). Our courses develop and refine students’ language skills while introducing them to the history, politics, and cultures of France and the French-speaking world.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in German Studies
Description: German Studies is an interdisciplinary program that includes the study of history, literature, film, philosophy, political science, music, and art. The major in German studies provides a broad humanistic education in the language, literature, and culture of the German-speaking countries. Students will develop their linguistic skills in German as a basis for further study, as well as their critical thinking and writing skills in English. Students may choose to focus their studies in German literature and culture, or they may want to complement their study of German with a focus on intellectual history or another national literature. Many German Studies majors combine their studies with a second major in another field such as government, history, economics, music, or engineering.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Global & Public Health Sciences
Concentration: ['Nutrition', 'Epidemiology', 'Physiology and the Human Body', 'Human Health & Social/Behavioral Sciences', 'Health Policy and Management']
Description: The Global and Public Health Sciences (GPHS) major, offered by the College of Human Ecology, provides a strong foundation in the life sciences and social sciences that prepares students for careers in public health. The interdisciplinary curriculum integrates a strong liberal arts education with a wide range of public health-related courses. Students interested in the pre-medical track should also consult with a pre-health advisor. Students interested in the program should contact dnsstudentservices@cornell.edu.

The major in government is designed to acquaint students with the theory and practice of politics at the local, state, national, and international levels. The department offers a wide array of courses, which are divided into four subfields: American politics, comparative politics, political theory, and international relations. The major is designed to be flexible so that students can construct a program of study that is tailored to their specific interests.

Concentration: Geographic concentrations: Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, Middle East/North Africa, United States. Thematic concentrations: History of Capitalism, History of Science and Technology, Law and Society, Race and Empire, Women, Gender, and Sexuality
Description: The history major is designed to be a versatile, flexible, liberal arts major. The program is designed to develop students’ analytical and writing skills, allowing them to explore specific historical interests and to acquire a broad understanding of the past and a sympathy with the people of other times and places.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in History of Architecture
Description: The undergraduate major in the History of Architecture offers an opportunity to study the history of the built environment in a vibrant intellectual community. Our flexible curriculum allows students to work closely with faculty members on a wide range of topics, from ancient to modern. We explore not only buildings but also cities, landscapes, and other designed objects. Our courses examine the relationships between architecture and social, cultural, political, economic, and technological histories around the globe. This approach prepares our students for a variety of careers and graduate programs, including architecture, landscape architecture, city and regional planning, historic preservation, real estate, arts administration, law, business, and medicine.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Hotel Administration
Department: Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration
Concentration: ['Finance, Accounting, and Real Estate (FARE)', 'Hospitality Leadership (HLDR)', 'Services Marketing and Operations Management (SMOM)']
Description:
The Nolan School of Hotel Administration is the world’s premier hospitality management school. The school’s mission is to create and disseminate knowledge about hospitality management through teaching, research, industry relations, and service. The school is an internationally recognized leader in the study of hospitality management, and its alumni are leaders and innovators in every facet of the global hospitality industry.

The hospitality industry is the largest in the world, and it is a dynamic and exciting industry in which to build a career. It includes a wide range of fields: hotel and resort operations, real estate and finance, food and beverage management, marketing, entrepreneurship, and much more. The Nolan School curriculum is comprehensive and provides students with a broad business education that is specifically focused on the hospitality industry.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Human Biology, Health, and Society
Description: The Human Biology, Health, and Society (HBHS) major provides a strong background in human biology, while preparing students to explore health issues from a social science perspective. The major is designed for students who are interested in careers in the health-care field, as physicians, dentists, veterinarians, or other health professionals, and for students who are interested in health policy, or a combination of these. Students will learn the basic biological sciences as well as the social and behavioral sciences that are relevant to human health. Students also learn how our social and physical environments can influence our health and well-being. This major integrates well with requirements for admission to most medical, dental and other health professional schools. With a strong grounding in biology, courses are available in human growth and development, anatomy, physiology, genetics, biochemistry, and nutrition. Complementary courses in the social sciences include human development, psychology, sociology and public health, which can lead to a rich understanding of human health in a social and ethical context.
ScholarshipType: Cornell grants, endowed scholarships, student employment

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Human Development
Description: Human Development majors explore the psychological, social, cultural, and biological development of people from conception through old age. The department’s five-area curriculum (Aging and Health; Cognitive Development; Human Developmental Behavioral Neuroscience; Law and Human Development; and Social and Personality Development) gives students a strong foundation in the behavioral sciences, while allowing them to pursue their specific interests. The major prepares students for a wide variety of careers in both the public and private sectors, including law, medicine, public health, social work, business, and education.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Industrial and Labor Relations
Department: School of Industrial and Labor Relations
Description: The School of Industrial and Labor Relations (ILR) is the world’s leading college of the applied social sciences focusing on work, employment, and labor policy issues in the U.S. and abroad. The ILR School’s undergraduate curriculum provides a strong foundation in the social sciences with a specific focus on the world of work. Drawing from the fields of economics, history, law, political science, psychology, and sociology, students learn to analyze and solve problems from a variety of perspectives. ILR’s flexible curriculum allows students to pursue a wide range of academic interests and professional goals.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Information Science
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences; College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: Behavioral Science (BEH), Computational Social Science (CSS), Data Science (DATA), Digital Culture and Production (DCP), Ethics, Law, and Policy (ELP), Information Science and Technology (IST), Networks, Crowds, and Markets (NCM), UX Design (UX), Individualized Concentration (IND)
Description:
Information Science (IS) is the study of how people and technology interact, and how technology can be used to address social, cultural, economic, and organizational issues. Information Science unites a variety of methods and theories from the social sciences, computer science, and humanities. It looks at system design as a human-centered, socially-aware process, using technology to solve problems in a wide variety of human contexts.

IS majors are leaders at the intersection of information, technology, and people. Majors develop a strong theoretical and methodological foundation in information science to become leaders in an information-rich world. The major has a strong technical core that is balanced with a focus on the social and cultural impact of technology. Students who major in information science have a passion to not only build the next great app but also to understand how the apps we use are changing us, our relationships, and our world.

Students who complete the major go on to a wide variety of careers, including user experience design, data science, product management, and software engineering at top technology companies such as Google, Meta, Apple, and Amazon. Others have started their own companies or become leaders in non-profits or the government. Many students go on to graduate school in a variety of fields, including information science, computer science, law, and business.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Information Science
Department: College of Arts and Sciences, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Fees: $68,380/Year (Endowed colleges); $46,396/Year (Statutory colleges, NYS residents) or $68,380/Year (Statutory colleges, out-of-state)
Concentration: Data Science, Digital Culture and Production, Information Ethics, Law, and Policy, Information Science, Systems, and Technology, Interactive Technologies, Networks, Crowds, and Markets, User Experience, Behavioral Science
Description: Information Science (IS) is the study of information and its role in the world. As an academic discipline, it is concerned with the processes of information creation, representation, organization, and retrieval, as well as the work information does in the social, cultural, economic, and political spheres. With its focus on computing and communication technologies, the field of IS has a strong design component: IS students learn how to build the systems that help us to create, manage and use information more effectively. The IS major is based in an interdisciplinary curriculum that combines computing and communication, social and cultural analysis, and design. Students take courses in three core areas: Content and Systems, Human and Social Systems, and Design. Students then choose an IS concentration and a set of electives based on their interests.
CostPerCredit: $2,849 (Endowed colleges); $1,933 (Statutory colleges, NYS residents) or $2,849 (Statutory colleges, out-of-state)

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Information Science, Systems, and Technology
Concentration: Digital Culture and Production, Data Science, Information Ethics, Law, and Policy, Interactive Technologies, Networks, Crowds, and Markets
Description: Information is a critical resource in all fields, so understanding how it is created, processed, stored, and retrieved is essential in the 21st century. The Information Science, Systems, and Technology (ISST) major provides a strong foundation in the technical aspects of information and information systems, including the mathematical and theoretical foundations of information science, data structures, algorithms, programming, and systems analysis and design. In the advanced curriculum students explore topics such as machine learning, data mining, user-centered design and development, network science, data science, and information ethics and policy. This combination prepares ISST majors for a variety of challenging technology careers, while at the same time giving them a perspective on the societal and human implications of their work.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Interdisciplinary Studies
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: The Interdisciplinary Studies major, leading to a B.S. degree, provides an opportunity for students to formulate a program of study to meet educational and career goals not accommodated by other majors in the college. The program is developed by the student in consultation with a faculty advisor and is approved by the college’s Interdisciplinary Studies Program Committee. The program must be a coherent, integrated course of study that is both interdisciplinary and focused. It may not be a random assortment of courses.
ScholarshipType: Cornell grants, endowed scholarships, loans, and employment

Description: The Italian major provides a course of study that is at once focused and flexible. Students majoring in Italian develop an excellent command of the Italian language and gain a deep knowledge of Italian literature and culture from the Middle Ages to the present. The major fosters skills in critical reading, thinking, and writing that are valuable in a wide variety of professions. The major consists of nine courses in Italian language, literature, and culture at the 2000 level and above. Of these nine courses, a minimum of five must be literature and culture courses at the 3000 level or above taught in Italian. Of these five courses, at least one must be dedicated to Dante, and at least one must focus on the medieval or early modern period (not including the Dante course), and at least one must focus on the modern or contemporary period. Courses taken to fulfill the major requirements must be taken for a letter grade and students must receive a grade of C or better. Courses must be chosen in consultation with the major advisor.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Landscape Architecture
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: The B.S. in Landscape Architecture is a four-year design degree housed in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. This STEM-designated program is fully accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board (LAAB). In the U.S. and many other countries, you must graduate from a LAAB-accredited program to become a licensed landscape architect. The program’s core curriculum gives students a solid foundation in the skills necessary for professional practice and advanced studies. At the core of the curriculum is a sequence of eight design studios. Each studio focuses on a specific design topic and builds on previous studios. For example, topics include site grading and engineering, planting design, land use planning, design for climate change, and urban design. In each studio, students learn a variety of design processes, theories, and techniques. Studio instruction is complemented by a series of required courses in topics such as landscape history, plants and ecology, site construction and technologies, and visual representation. Professional practice courses prepare students for the contemporary workplace, and the curriculum is regularly updated to include the latest technologies used in the field. Beyond the core curriculum, students must choose a number of liberal arts courses, and they are encouraged to select a series of electives from landscape architecture and other disciplines at Cornell. By carefully selecting electives, students can develop a focus in areas such as ecological design, community design, urban design, or landscape art. To gain an expanded perspective on the landscape and its diverse cultural meanings, students are strongly encouraged to study abroad in their junior or senior year. In the Department of Landscape Architecture, the faculty are internationally recognized experts in their fields, including ecological design, urban design and place-making, community engagement, climate change adaptation, landscape history and theory, drawing and visual representation, and advanced digital technologies.
Accredidation: This STEM-designated program is fully accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board (LAAB).

Description: Linguistics is the systematic study of human language. The linguistics major is concerned with the nature of human language, its function, structure, and history. Students learn how to analyze language and languages, from the level of sound to the level of sentence structure and discourse, through core courses in phonology, syntax, and semantics. Through the study of historical linguistics, they learn how languages change and evolve. Elective courses in linguistics provide students with opportunities to explore a range of topics including the study of meaning, computational linguistics, language acquisition, sociolinguistics, and psycholinguistics, as well as the study of specific languages or language families. Many students combine a major in linguistics with a major in another field, such as psychology, cognitive science, computer science, philosophy, anthropology, or the language-and-area studies programs.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Materials Science and Engineering
Concentration: ['Biomaterials', 'Ceramics', 'Composites', 'Electronic Materials', 'Energy Materials', 'Metals', 'Nanomaterials', 'Polymers']
Description: Materials science and engineering (MSE) is an interdisciplinary field that applies the principles of basic sciences and engineering to the design and creation of new materials. Nearly every engineering discipline and all of modern technology is in some way dependent on materials. Materials scientists and engineers work on problems as diverse as designing stronger alloys for more fuel-efficient airplanes, creating new semiconductors for faster computer chips, developing new biocompatible materials for better medical implants, and creating new battery and fuel cell materials for a greener energy future. The MSE curriculum covers the fundamental science of materials as well as a broad range of engineering applications. Students have extensive opportunities to participate in research with world-renowned faculty in state-of-the-art facilities.
Accredidation: The Materials Science and Engineering (B.S.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org, under the General Criteria and the Program Criteria for Materials, Metallurgical, Metallurgical and Materials, and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.

Concentration: Standard Mathematics Major, Computer Science Concentration, Economics Concentration, Operations Research Concentration, Pure and Applied Mathematics Concentration
Description: Mathematics is the language of modern science. It is a human endeavor that has spanned cultures and centuries. It is a way of thinking, a discipline of mind, and an art form. It is one of the great liberal arts, and it is a skill essential for a growing number of careers. Cornell’s mathematics program is recognized as one of the best in the world. The department’s undergraduate program is a lively and multi-faceted one that offers a large variety of courses and several different options within the major. Our students go on to be leaders in academia, business, government, and a wide array of other fields. The major is flexible enough to be compatible with the needs of students who want a deep and extensive training in mathematics and also with the needs of students who would like to combine the study of mathematics with a major or minor in another field. Many mathematics majors take a double major in another field, for example in computer science, biology, economics, and physics.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering
Description: Mechanical engineering is one of the broadest of the engineering disciplines. It is concerned with the design, manufacture, and operation of a wide range of components, devices, and systems. Mechanical engineers are involved with energy conversion and fluid and thermal sciences; machine design, manufacturing, and control; and materials behavior and processing. The Sibley School curriculum is designed to provide a broad background in these areas and to offer a number of specializations. The undergraduate program is a preparation for a wide range of careers including industry, government, research, and graduate study. Mechanical engineers are employed in nearly every industry. These include major established industries such as aerospace, automotive, bio-medical devices, chemical, electronics, materials, and petroleum, as well as many emerging areas such as biotechnology, environmental engineering, nanotechnology, and sustainable energy. The Sibley School does not require students to declare a focus area, but most students will naturally gravitate to a few areas and many do undergraduate research or project work in these areas.
Accredidation: The Mechanical Engineering (M.E.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.

Description:
The B.A. in music is a liberal arts degree. It provides a thorough grounding in the discipline while allowing students flexibility to pursue a wide variety of other interests inside and outside music. Some B.A. students have a second major in another field. Many others have no other major, but take a wide variety of courses in other disciplines while concentrating in music. This degree is not primarily intended for those who wish to prepare for a career as a professional performer, although some graduates of this program do go on to such careers. Rather, the B.A. is for those who are passionate about music and wish it to be the focus of their undergraduate studies, but who are not yet sure what career they might wish to pursue after graduation. In this way, the B.A. keeps many options open.

Students contemplating graduate study in music are encouraged to study at least one foreign language (typically German or French) as part of their undergraduate curriculum. Students who wish to pursue the B.A. degree with a specific area of focus (composition, history, theory, or performance) should work closely with their advisors to select an appropriate combination of courses. Students who wish to focus on performance may, upon application and audition, be admitted to the B.A. degree with honors in music.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Near Eastern Studies
Concentration: ['Language, Literature, and Culture', 'History, Archaeology, and Politics', 'Jewish Studies']
Description: The major in Near Eastern studies is a liberal arts program that provides students with a broad knowledge of the cultures, languages, history, and religions of the Middle East from antiquity to the modern day. The department offers courses in Near Eastern archaeology, history, languages, literatures, and religions, as well as on a variety of special topics. A major in Near Eastern studies prepares students for careers in the U.S. government (the Foreign Service and other agencies), in journalism, in business in or relating to the Middle East, and in various non-governmental organizations. The major also provides an excellent basis for graduate study in the various disciplines of Middle Eastern studies. The department also offers minors in Near Eastern studies and in Jewish studies.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Nutritional Sciences
Department: College of Human Ecology, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration:
Dietetics
Global and Public Health
Human Nutrition, Health, and Society
Description: The Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in Nutritional Sciences degree program in the Division of Nutritional Sciences is a flexible and broad-based program that allows students to fulfill pre-health course requirements and explore the broad field of nutritional sciences from a basic biological science and/or social/behavioral science perspective. Graduates of the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences program are eligible for graduate study in a wide variety of fields, including biological sciences, nutritional sciences, medicine, dentistry, and other allied health fields, and other professional schools, such as public health, business, or law. Additionally, graduates are prepared for employment in health-related professions, in the food industry, and in community nutrition. The program is offered to students in both the College of Human Ecology (CHE) and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). The information that follows pertains to students who are matriculated in the College of Human Ecology. Students interested in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences should reference the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences CALS page. Although the admission requirements differ between colleges, the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences curriculum is the same for all students, regardless of their college. Once matriculated, students may not transfer from one college to the other. Although the core curriculum is the same, each college has its own graduation requirements; the information on this page is for students for whom the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences is housed in the College of Human Ecology.
Accredidation: The Didactic Program in Dietetics (DPD) at Cornell University is accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 120 South Riverside Plaza, Suite 2190, Chicago, IL 60606-6995, (312) 899-0040 ext. 5400. http://www.eatrightpro.org/ACEND. Effective January 1, 2024, the Commission on Dietetic Registration (CDR) will require a minimum of a master’s degree to be eligible to take the credentialing exam to become a registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN).

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Operations Research and Engineering
Concentration: ['Academic Concentration', 'Applied Operations Research Concentration', 'Data Analytics Concentration', 'Financial Engineering Concentration', 'Information Science and Technology Concentration', 'Strategic and Management Science Concentration']
Description: Operations Research and Engineering (ORE) is the engineering discipline that deals with the application of advanced analytical methods to help make better decisions. It is a diverse field that is also referred to as "the science of better". The ORE major at Cornell is designed to provide students with a strong foundation in the technical and mathematical tools of the discipline with an emphasis on their practical application in a variety of settings. Students learn and become proficient in the core skills of the discipline including mathematical modeling, optimization, probability, statistics, and simulation, as well as in the application areas of manufacturing, supply chain management, financial engineering, and data analytics. Students are encouraged to develop a concentration in a particular area of interest. The ORE major is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.
Accredidation: The ORE major is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Performing and Media Arts
Concentration: Theatre and Performance; Cinema and Media Studies; Dance; customized concentration
Description: The Department of Performing and Media Arts (PMA) is a community of artists and scholars who share a commitment to the arts as a vital component of intellectual and cultural life. We believe in the power of live performance and mediated art to stimulate the imagination, foster debate, and enrich our understanding of the world. Our mission is to educate a new generation of artists and scholars to think critically and creatively about the arts, to produce work that is both innovative and socially engaged, and to lead the way in a rapidly changing cultural landscape. The Department offers a diverse curriculum in theatre, performance studies, cinema and media studies, and dance that explores the arts from a variety of perspectives—historical, theoretical, and practical. We offer a major in Performing and Media Arts that leads to the B.A. degree as well as a minor in theatre, a minor in dance, and a minor in film. We also produce a full season of plays, dance concerts, and film screenings each year that provide opportunities for students to apply what they have learned in the classroom to the stage and screen. These productions are an integral part of our educational mission and a major contribution to the cultural life of the Cornell community.

Philosophy is the rational investigation of fundamental questions about the nature of reality, the mind, and the value. These questions are not the province of any of the special sciences; rather, they are the most general and abstract questions that can be asked. Philosophy is also the study of the methods of rational investigation of such questions, i.e. of the principles of logic and epistemology. And it is the study of the history of philosophical thought.

The philosophy curriculum at Cornell helps students to think, read, and write clearly and critically. The courses offer a broad and deep education in the liberal arts, and many of them have a strong interdisciplinary component, connecting philosophy with literature, history, law, mathematics, and the sciences. Philosophical study is excellent preparation for a wide variety of professional and business careers, including law, medicine, finance, journalism, education, and public service.

The Department of Physics offers a full range of university-level work in physics, from general education courses for nonscientists to doctoral-level independent research. The department’s goal is to provide students with a rich and varied education in physics and related subjects.

Physics is the study of the fundamental laws of nature. The beauty and mystery of these laws can be appreciated at many levels, from the most qualitative to the most quantitative. The department is committed to helping students with a wide range of interests and abilities to see the world from a physicist’s perspective.

A major in physics can prepare a student for a variety of careers. Some physics majors go on to graduate school in physics or a related field, leading to a career in research and/or teaching. Others go to professional school (law, medicine, and business are the most common). Still others go directly into the work force, in areas as diverse as computer programming, finance, and technical writing. The physics major provides an excellent general-purpose technical education.

The BA degree is a liberal arts degree. It is well suited for students who want a physics background for a career in another field such as medicine, law, or business, or for students who want to combine the study of physics with another discipline.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Plant Sciences
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Fees: New York State Residents: $45,888/Year; Out-of-State Residents: $68,380/Year
Concentration: ['Plant Biology', 'Plant Breeding and Genetics', 'Plant Pathology and Plant-Microbe Biology', 'Plant Physiology', 'Sustainable Plant Production', 'Soil Science', 'Ecology of Managed Landscapes']
Description: The Plant Sciences Major provides students with a fundamental and applied understanding of how plants work. Plants are at the foundation of all life on earth. They convert the sun’s energy into food and fiber, and they provide ecosystem services that clean our air and water. Plant scientists study plants at all levels of organization, from molecules to ecosystems, to understand how plants grow, reproduce, and interact with other organisms in a changing environment. This knowledge is used to sustainably produce food, fiber, and fuel for a growing world population and to conserve our natural ecosystems. Our majors are curious, problem-solving people with interests that range from social justice to conservation biology, from molecular biology to agroecology, and from improving human nutrition to increasing the aesthetic value of plants. Students choose to major in plant sciences because they will be able to make an impact in the world by addressing the grand challenges facing humanity, including food security, climate change, human health, and environmental stewardship.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Policy Analysis and Management
Department: Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy
Concentration: Public Policy, Health Policy
Description: The Policy Analysis and Management (PAM) major provides a multi-disciplinary, applied-social science education in public policy. PAM students develop a fundamental understanding of the policy process as well as the economic and sociological theories that can be used to analyze, design, and implement policies in the public, private and nonprofit sectors. PAM majors also learn the statistical and research methods that are needed to conduct rigorous policy analysis. The major prepares students to think critically about public policy and provides a strong foundation for a variety of careers and for graduate school. Many graduates enter law school or earn graduate degrees in public policy, health administration, or business. Those graduates who go directly to work are employed in a wide variety of settings in the public, nonprofit, and private sectors.

Psychology is the science of the mind and of behavior. The Psychology major is designed to provide students with a broad overview of the different approaches to the study of psychology. Within the major, we offer four different areas of study:

Perception, Cognition and Development (PCD): focuses on the fundamental aspects of the mind, including how we perceive and remember information, how we acquire and use language, and how our perceptual and cognitive abilities change throughout our lives.

Behavioral and Evolutionary Neuroscience (BEN): focuses on the biological basis of behavior, including the neural circuits responsible for our perceptions, memories, and actions, and how these systems have been shaped by evolutionary pressures.

Social and Personality Psychology (S&P): focuses on the psychology of everyday life, including why we are attracted to certain people, how we are influenced by groups, and how we form our attitudes and beliefs.

The courses offered by the department reflect the diversity of the field. They range from the study of the brain, to the study of the mind, to the study of individual and group behavior. The major is structured to ensure that students become familiar with the methods of psychological inquiry, as well as the different areas of the field.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Religious Studies
Description: The Religious Studies Program offers students the opportunity to study the religions of the world in a secular, academic setting. The program is interdisciplinary, drawing on the perspectives of the humanities and social sciences. Students in the program learn about the history, sacred texts, beliefs and practices of the world’s religions, and they also learn how to think critically about religion as a historical and cultural phenomenon. The curriculum is designed to be both broad and deep, allowing students to combine a general overview of the field with a more specialized focus on a particular religious tradition, a specific geographical area, or a critical theme in the study of religion.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Science & Technology Studies
Concentration: ['Environment and Sustainability', 'Global and Transnational STS', 'Health, Medicine, and Society', 'Mind, Information, and Intelligence']
Description:
Science and technology are defining features of modern societies, but their social and cultural significance is a matter of intense debate. Science and Technology Studies (STS) is a field that seeks to understand the social, political, and cultural dimensions of science and technology in the modern world. STS uses methods from a variety of disciplines, including history, sociology, philosophy, anthropology, and political science, to study how science and technology both shape and are shaped by their social contexts.

The STS major is designed for students who wish to pursue a liberal arts education in this field. Students in the major explore a variety of topics, such as the history of scientific discovery and technological innovation; the relationship between science, technology and public policy; the social and ethical implications of new technologies; and the role of science and technology in non-western societies.

Sociology is the study of social life, social change, and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations, and societies, and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to the hostile mob; from organized crime to religious traditions; from the divisions of race, gender, and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The undergraduate major in sociology provides students with a firm understanding of the discipline’s theories and methods and allows students to explore their own areas of interest in the discipline.

The Spanish major is designed to give students a thorough grounding in the language and a broad introduction to the literatures and cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. The major in Spanish provides an area of concentration for students who wish to specialize in the language, literature, and culture of the Spanish-speaking world. Satisfying the requirements for a major in Spanish can lead to a variety of careers in which a sound knowledge of the language and culture is a distinct advantage (e.g., international law, business, journalism, diplomacy, and education).

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Statistical Science
Description:
The undergraduate major in Statistical Science, which is available to students in the College of Arts and Sciences and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, provides a rigorous education in all aspects of statistics, from theoretical to applied. Students majoring in statistical science can take a broad range of courses, allowing them to not only be well-grounded in the fundamentals of the field but also to explore more advanced topics.

Students who complete the major in statistical science will have a wide range of career opportunities, including in banking and finance, the insurance industry, medical and pharmaceutical research, big tech and advertising, manufacturing, and government agencies, to name a few. In addition, students who graduate with a major in statistical science will be very well-prepared to enter a graduate program in statistics or a related field.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Urban and Regional Studies
Department: College of Architecture, Art, and Planning
Description: The Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in Urban and Regional Studies (URS) is a pre-professional degree that prepares students to enter a master's degree program in city and regional planning. The curriculum for the B.S. degree is similar to the requirements of the first year of a master's program in city and regional planning. The B.S. degree combines a strong liberal arts base with a concentration in the theory and practice of urban and regional studies. A key feature of the degree is the multi-disciplinary approach to the study of urban areas and the planning process. Students have the opportunity to take classes in six different Cornell colleges, in addition to the core classes in CRP. Students complete a total of 120 credit hours to graduate.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Viticulture and Enology
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Concentration: Enology, Viticulture, Economics and Business
Description: The Viticulture and Enology (VE) major, offered by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, prepares students for a variety of careers in the grape and wine industry. The curriculum provides a strong background in the basic sciences, an extensive theoretical and practical background in viticulture and enology through a core series of courses, and the opportunity for students to specialize in one discipline. Students are prepared for careers in vineyard management, winemaking, business, and research and extension. The VE program is offered as a collaboration between Cornell University and our educational partner, Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, New York. Students spend most of their first two years on the Ithaca campus, and they must spend at least one semester at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva to complete required coursework.

Department: Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science
Description: The Department of Statistical Science and the Department of Mathematics jointly offer a minor in Actuarial Science for students who want to prepare for a career in the actuarial field. To be successful in this field, it is important to have a strong background in mathematics and statistics, as well as some knowledge of economics and finance. These subject areas are the foundations of the actuarial profession. Actuaries are experts in the management of uncertainty and risk. The primary function of an actuary is to determine the value of future financial obligations, such as the benefits provided by an insurance policy or pension plan. Doing this requires an in-depth understanding of not just the mathematics of probability and statistics, but also of finance and economics. By successfully completing the Actuarial Science minor, students will have the background to take and pass the first two professional examinations given by the Society of Actuaries (SOA) and the Casualty Actuarial Society (CAS). These are Exam P/1 (Probability) and Exam FM/2 (Financial Mathematics). Students will also be well-prepared to complete the SOA Validation by Educational Experience (VEE) requirements in Economics, Corporate Finance, and Applied Statistical Methods.

The Aerospace Engineering minor provides a formal structure for Cornell undergraduates who want to pursue a career in the aerospace industry or in a related research and development field. The curriculum provides a broad background in the scientific and engineering principles of aerospace engineering. Topics include fluid mechanics, aerodynamics, propulsion, structures, and dynamics and control.

The Africana Studies minor is intended for students who are interested in the study of the peoples of African descent in the United States, the Caribbean, Latin America, Europe and Africa. The curriculum of the minor is structured across three subfields within Africana Studies: African-American studies; continental African studies; and Caribbean/Latin American studies. The purpose of the minor is to provide a comprehensive, interdisciplinary, and focused study of the Africana experience.

ProgramName: American Indian and Indigenous Studies Minor
Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: The American Indian and Indigenous Studies Program (AIISP) offers a minor in American Indian and Indigenous Studies (AIIS). The minor provides an interdisciplinary framework for the study of the history, culture, and contemporary lives of Indigenous peoples of the Americas. The curriculum offers a rich mix of courses, which can be combined to create a course of study that is continental or hemispheric, and that can include a focus on a particular region, nation, or theme. The minor seeks to prepare students to work in a wide variety of fields both within and outside Indigenous communities. It offers a solid foundation for those students who may wish to pursue graduate work in the fields of American Indian and Indigenous studies, law, education, social work, cultural resource management, or other academic or professional fields.

The American Sign Language (ASL)/Deaf Studies minor, offered through the Department of Linguistics, consists of 15 credits of course work. The minor provides a coherent program of study in the language and culture of the Deaf. The minor is meant for any undergraduate student at Cornell who has an interest in ASL, Deaf studies, Deaf culture, or a related area.

The American Studies Minor at Cornell provides a framework for students who want to develop their understanding of the complex texture of American culture, society and politics, past and present. The program serves students who are curious about the nation’s history, who want to make sense of the diversity of American experiences and who want to critically engage the meanings of “America.” Drawing on a wide range of courses and faculty from across the university, the minor encourages students to think across disciplinary boundaries to ask new and better questions about the United States, in all of its complexity and contradiction. American Studies students may focus on a particular historical period, a specific social group, a particular region, or a theme like law, social justice, performance, or visual culture. The program provides students with the critical and analytical tools to understand American identity, culture, and power in a global context.

Department: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: The Animal Science minor is designed for students who have an interest in animal biology and the management of domestic animals. The curriculum provides a strong foundation in the basic sciences that are a prerequisite to many of the applied courses in animal science. A flexible curriculum, it allows for a diverse number of courses to be taken to fulfill requirements, which can serve the student with either a casual interest or a strong career goal in the animal sciences. The Department of Animal Science has more than 40 faculty members with a wide range of expertise, from molecular biology to farm management. Many of these faculty members are available to serve as advisors to students who select the minor.
ScholarshipType: Cornell grants, endowed scholarships, loans, work-study

Description: The minor in Anthropology provides a structured yet flexible program for students to explore the field of anthropology alongside other intellectual interests. With its signature focus on cross-cultural comparison, the minor is an excellent complement to a range of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences. The minor helps students cultivate a critical perspective on their own society and an appreciation for the diversity of human worlds.

Department: Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management
Description: The Applied Economics Minor provides students with a systematic way of thinking about economic decisions that can be used in a wide variety of settings. The minor provides a framework for analyzing and understanding a broad range of economic issues, such as those related to management, marketing, finance, production, environment, and development. The tools and concepts learned are relevant to a broad range of real-world problems and situations as they relate to business, government, non-profits, and other settings.

Department: School of Integrative Plant Science, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
Description: The Applied Exercise Science (AES) minor is housed in the Division of Nutritional Sciences and provides students with a strong foundation in the anatomical, biomechanical, and physiological responses to exercise and physical activity. Students will have opportunities for hands-on learning in the Human Metabolic Research Unit’s Bod Pod and DEXA scan, teaching laboratories, and through applied research projects. The minor provides foundational knowledge for students interested in a variety of careers including physical therapy, occupational therapy, physician’s assistant, medicine, athletic training, and other allied health professions. It can also enhance the education of students with a general interest in health, fitness and athletic performance. The minor is a valuable complement to majors including nutritional sciences; human biology, health, and society; global and public health sciences; biological sciences; and human development, as it provides a unique focus on the application of scientific principles to human movement, exercise, and nutritional sciences.

The Applied Mathematics minor provides the student with a strong background in the techniques of applied mathematics. The prerequisites for the minor are MATH 1910, MATH 1920, MATH 2930, and MATH 2940, or their equivalents. Note that many courses in applied mathematics require some programming knowledge. The minor requires a total of six courses of three or more credits, chosen from approved course lists in two groups, as follows: 1) Three courses from Group A (3000-level), one of which must be an analysis course and one of which must be an algebra course; and 2) Three courses from Group B (4000-level), two of which must be a two-course sequence. The courses are listed under Center for Applied Mathematics. Substitutions for these courses may be approved by the Director of Undergraduate Studies.

The minor in Arabic provides students with a solid foundation in the Arabic language and introduces them to the cultures of the Arabic-speaking world. The minor consists of five courses, three of which must be at the 3000-level or above. Students must take one Arabic language course at the 3000 level or above. No more than one course may be taken in a related field and at the discretion of the Arabic program director. Of these five courses, at least three must be taken at Cornell. A grade of C or better is required for all courses to count toward the minor.
ScholarshipType: Need-based grants, student loans, student employment

Description: Archaeology is a quintessentially interdisciplinary field, drawing on the sciences, the social sciences, and the humanities to understand the human past. The Archaeology Minor offers a framework for constructing a coherent program of study in archaeology from the wide-ranging offerings of a number of different departments and programs. Students in the minor will achieve a solid grounding in archaeological method, theory and practice in their core courses, and then will build a particular specialization within a chosen area of emphasis.

The Department of Architecture in the College of Architecture, Art, and Planning offers a minor in architecture to undergraduate students in all colleges at Cornell. The minor provides a basic understanding of architecture and its relationship to the arts and sciences. The minor is not a pre-professional program of study and does not qualify students for admission to a graduate program in architecture. Students are admitted to the minor by the Department of Architecture.

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) minor is a new cross-college undergraduate minor that guides students in the study of the core principles of AI, as well as its ethical and social implications. Students will learn about foundational AI topics, such as machine learning, search, and knowledge representation, and also delve into AI subfields, such as natural language processing, vision, and robotics. The minor will culminate with a project course in which students will work on a substantial, team-based AI project. The minor is a joint program offered by the College of Arts and Sciences, the College of Engineering, and the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. The minor is administered by the Cornell Bowers CIS Department of Computer Science.

The Asian American Studies Program (AASP) is a university-wide program housed in the College of Arts & Sciences. Its mission is to advance the study of Asian Americans and to promote a fuller understanding of the lived experiences of Asian Americans in a comparative and global perspective. The minor in Asian American studies is open to all undergraduate students at Cornell University. The curriculum establishes a foundation in the history and cultures of Asian Americans, explores theories and practices of race and ethnicity in relation to U.S. national and transnational contexts, and engages with the complexities of Asian American experiences and identities. AASP courses highlight the histories, communities, and cultures of Asians in the Americas, looking at a range of topics including labor, migration, and refugees; law, politics, and policy; empire, war, and militarism; gender and sexuality; media, performance, and the arts; and social movements and community empowerment. Overall, the program emphasizes interdisciplinary and comparative approaches to the study of race, ethnicity, and diaspora, and views Asian American studies as a field of power, knowledge, and social justice.

The minor in Astrobiology is intended for students with an interest in the astronomical, planetary, and biological sciences. The interdisciplinary field of astrobiology is concerned with the distribution of life in the universe, a topic that has generated enormous public interest and is now a focus of a wide array of scientific endeavors, including NASA missions. The courses in this minor provide the basic astronomical and biological background for students interested in this field, introduce them to current topics of research, and expose them to the interdisciplinary nature of the field.

The minor in astronomy is offered for students who are not majoring in the physical sciences but who wish to have a substantive understanding of the fundamentals of astronomy and astrophysics. The minor may also be of interest to physical science majors who wish to supplement their major with a broad-based introduction to astronomy and astrophysics.

The Atmospheric Sciences minor is designed to provide students with a coherent and substantive background in atmospheric sciences. The minor is sufficiently flexible that students can tailor a course sequence that builds upon their own interests and the strengths of their major fields of study. The minor requires a minimum of 18 credits. Courses selected must form a coherent program and be approved by an advisor in atmospheric sciences.

The minor in Biological Engineering is intended for students in engineering or the life sciences who are interested in the application of engineering and quantitative principles to biological systems. The minor provides a coherent program of study in biological engineering, enabling students to choose a curriculum that complements their major and prepares them for graduate study in biomedical and biological engineering and related fields, or for professional careers at the interface of engineering and biology.

The Biological Sciences minor is available to any undergraduate in any college at Cornell who is not majoring in biological sciences. The minor provides a way for students with an interest in biology to gain a broad background in the subject and exposure to the new discoveries that are rapidly advancing the field. To complete the minor, students take a minimum of five courses in biological sciences including a two-semester introductory biology sequence, an organismal biology course, and at least two other courses in biological sciences at the 2000 level or above. The two upper-level courses must be a minimum of 3 credits each. Students who complete the minor have the equivalent of approximately one semester of study in biological sciences. Completion of the minor will be noted on the student’s transcript.

The undergraduate minor in Biomedical Engineering (BME) provides students with a strong foundation in the concentration areas of biomedical engineering. The BME minor is available to all undergraduates in the College of Engineering and in the Colleges of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Arts and Sciences, and Human Ecology. For students in the College of Engineering, the BME minor is intended to be completed in conjunction with an accredited major. The BME minor will introduce students to the multidisciplinary aspects of biomedical engineering research and the diversity of the biomedical engineering profession. Students are expected to have completed ENGRD 2202 and MATH 2940 as part of their major requirements before admission to the minor. A grade of C or better is required for all courses in the minor.

The Department of Statistical Science offers a minor in Biometry and Statistics. This minor is intended for students in the life sciences and provides a coherent program of study in the application of statistical and mathematical methods to the life sciences. The minor is administered by the Director of Undergraduate Studies of the Statistical Science department, who will approve a course of study for the student. The minor requires at least 18 credits.

The university-wide business minor (BUS) is for students in any Cornell college or school other than the Dyson School or the Nolan School. The primary objective is to provide students with a broad understanding of business and the U.S. and world economies. Students in this minor will take courses that will prepare them to be business leaders, managers, and entrepreneurs. Requirements include four core courses and one elective course. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C or better must be received to count towards the minor.

The Business Minor for Engineers (BME) is an interdisciplinary program offered by the School of Operations Research and Information Engineering (ORIE) and the Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management (AEM). The minor provides a solid foundation of business principles particularly well-suited for engineering students, preparing them for a wide range of career opportunities.

Students pursuing the BME develop a strong understanding of business fundamentals in accounting, finance, marketing, and management, along with key skills in leadership, communication, and business ethics. These skills and knowledge will complement your engineering degree, enabling you to excel in technology-focused businesses or in a variety of other business settings.

The BME minor is available to any student majoring in the College of Engineering. For more information, please visit the Business Minor for Engineers website.

The Caribbean Studies Minor is an interdisciplinary undergraduate minor that provides students with an integrated, multicultural, and hemispheric approach to the study of the Caribbean. It seeks to study the Caribbean as a region of diverse societies that have been shaped by and have made significant contributions to the broader world. The minor encourages an interdisciplinary approach to the study of the Caribbean and works to promote intellectual exchange and dialogue among students and faculty from different disciplinary and departmental units at Cornell.

The minor in China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CAPS) is designed for students in all colleges who wish to develop a sophisticated understanding of contemporary China and its role in the Asia-Pacific region and the world. The CAPS program emphasizes social sciences, including applied economics and management, business, development sociology, government, and sociology. As one of the preeminent centers for the study of Chinese language, literature, and culture in the United States, Cornell offers more than 100 courses on China. The CAPS minor offers an interdisciplinary curriculum designed to provide students with a structured yet flexible program to study China’s expanding global influence.

The minor in Civil Infrastructure provides a coherent program of study for students interested in the design and management of the constructed environment. Civil infrastructure systems are the foundation of modern society. They include transportation systems (e.g., highways, airports, ports); water resource systems (e.g., water supply, flood control, irrigation); environmental protection systems (e.g., wastewater treatment, solid waste management); energy systems (e.g., electric power, oil and gas); and constructed facilities (e.g., buildings, bridges, and tunnels). The design, construction, and operation of these systems involve a wide range of considerations including engineering analysis, materials science, systems engineering, economics, and public policy. The minor is flexible, and can be tailored to an individual student’s interests. Students completing the minor will have a greater understanding of the challenges associated with developing and managing civil infrastructure systems, and be better prepared for careers that require such knowledge.

The minor in Classical civilization is for students who wish to pursue an interest in the history, literature, and culture of the ancient Mediterranean world. The minor requires a minimum of five courses (totaling at least 15 credits) chosen from offerings in Classical civilization, Classical languages, archaeology, ancient history, ancient philosophy, and other related subjects approved by the director of undergraduate studies. Language courses at the 3000-level or above can also count toward the minor. The specific courses that will satisfy the requirements are to be chosen in consultation with the director of undergraduate studies.

The Department of Classics at Cornell is devoted to the interdisciplinary study of Greek and Roman antiquity. We consider this the original “area studies” program, embracing all aspects of the ancient Mediterranean world, including the Greek and Roman languages, but also literature, history, philosophy, art history, archaeology, and ancient thought more generally. We welcome students from across the university with a wide array of interests. Our students have diverse aspirations and go on to careers in many fields, including law, medicine, finance, journalism, education, and the arts, in addition to professional work in Classics.
The Classics minor is for students who want to become more familiar with the ancient world while developing their intellectual skills for careers in many fields. It has very flexible requirements so that students can focus their studies in areas that most interest them.
The minor provides an opportunity to read some of the world’s greatest literature in English translation; discover how Greek and Roman cultures contributed to the development of world civilizations; and explore the ways in which Classical antiquity continues to shape our cultural identities.

The Climate Change Minor is a cross-college, cross-campus undergraduate minor available to all Cornell undergraduates. The minor is designed to develop a broad understanding of the Earth’s climate system; the ecological, economic, and social impacts of climate change on people and the planet; and the ethical, social and policy dimensions for developing and implementing solutions. It provides opportunities for students to study climate change through a diverse and interdisciplinary curriculum that bridges the physical and social sciences, humanities, and arts. The minor is hosted by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences in collaboration with the College of Arts & Sciences and the College of Engineering and administered by the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. Students can choose from more than 100 courses from over 30 departments in 7 colleges and schools to complete the minor. The Climate Change Minor requires at least 18 credits. Contact the Program Manager (climatechange@cornell.edu) for questions and help with planning the minor.

The Cognitive Science minor is designed for students who want to learn about the mind from an interdisciplinary perspective. The minor provides a framework for the integrated study of a variety of fields, including: psychology, computer science, linguistics, philosophy, neuroscience, and anthropology. Students must complete a core course in cognitive science and a set of five additional courses that provide a broad foundation in the various allied disciplines and a more focused study in a particular area of cognitive science.

The Communication minor is for students in any college at Cornell who are interested in the systematic study of human communication. The minor seeks to provide students with a strong foundation in communication theory and research, while also offering flexibility in the specific sub-areas in which they choose to specialize. Students who complete the minor will have a broad understanding of the communication discipline and will be able to apply communication theories and research to a wide range of social, political, and economic contexts. Students can apply to the Communication minor as early as their first semester of their sophomore year.

The minor in Community Food Systems (CFS) provides students with a strong foundation in the principles and practices of sustainable agriculture, and the economic, social, and political aspects of local food systems. The minor is designed to complement a number of majors in CALS and other colleges, and will prepare students for a diversity of careers related to food and agriculture, including farm and food business management, non-profit organizations, cooperative extension, and public policy. The CFS minor is administered by the SIPS Horticulture Section and is open to all Cornell undergraduates. It consists of a minimum of 16 credits.

The minor in Comparative Literature offers students a structured path into the discipline, its questions, and its methodologies. It is often a first step toward more advanced work in literature, theory, and cultural studies. It can be an excellent complement to a wide range of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences. For students interested in the minor, please visit complit.cornell.edu or contact the Director of Undergraduate Studies, Professor Ewa Domańska (ed349@cornell.edu).

The Department of Computer Science offers a minor in computer science for students in any college at Cornell. The minor is designed for students who have a serious interest in the subject but do not have the time to complete a major. The requirements are designed to provide a firm grounding in the fundamentals of computer science.

The Creative Writing Minor offers undergraduates a structured opportunity to develop their craft and knowledge of literary expression. Students in the minor will work with a faculty advisor to develop a course of study that best suits their individual needs as writers and readers.

ProgramName: Crime, Prisons, Education, and Justice Minor
Description: The Crime, Prisons, Education, and Justice minor (CPEJ) provides an opportunity for students to learn about the problems of crime, criminal justice, and mass incarceration in the United States, with an emphasis on the differing perspectives of social science, law, and the humanities. The CPEJ minor has two major goals. The first is to help students analyze the American criminal justice system in its historical and comparative context, and to examine its social, economic, and cultural determinants and effects. The second goal is to expose students to the educational and restorative practices that might help the criminal justice system better serve its multiple functions of promoting public safety, providing justice to victims, and rehabilitating those who have committed crimes. Students in the CPEJ minor will learn about the challenges our society faces in relation to crime and punishment, and also about the work being done on campus and around the country to improve the lives of those affected by crime and incarceration.

The Crop Management minor is an undergraduate minor administered through the Soil and Crop Sciences Section of the School of Integrative Plant Science. The minor provides a systematic program of study of the scientific principles and practices of crop management. The minor provides sufficient flexibility for students to focus their interests on a particular commodity group (e.g. food crops, forage crops, or turfgrass), or on a particular discipline (e.g. crop physiology and ecology, soil management, or integrated pest management). Students who complete the minor will have an excellent background for work in crop production and related industries, and for graduate school in an applied plant science. This minor is not available to students majoring in Plant Sciences, Agricultural Sciences with a crop production concentration, or students majoring in the Viticulture and Enology program through the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

The Dance minor offers students an opportunity to explore dance as a cultural and artistic practice. Course offerings in the dance minor give students a wide range of experiences, including dance technique, choreography, performance, and the historical and cultural study of dance forms. The curriculum is designed for students who wish to pursue a serious and comprehensive study of dance within the context of a liberal arts education. Students may focus their studies in the dance minor on particular areas of interest such as composition, performance, or cultural and historical studies. Students interested in the dance minor should contact the Director of Dance.

The Data Science in Astronomy Minor is an interdisciplinary minor offered by the Astronomy department for students in any Cornell college. This minor applies data science techniques to big data sets in astronomy. This minor is not open to students majoring in Statistical Science or students minoring in Statistical Science.

The Data Science (DS) minor is an undergraduate program available to students in all colleges at the Ithaca campus. Data Science is an expanding field that requires substantive expertise in an application domain and knowledge of computational, statistical, and mathematical data analysis. The DS minor will provide students with the key skills and knowledge for data-driven inquiry. Completion of the minor will be recorded on the student’s official transcript.

The Demography Minor provides undergraduates with a strong foundation in the concepts, methods, and substantive findings of population studies. Students learn how to analyze demographic data and understand how population processes are affected by and have consequences for social, economic, political, and cultural phenomena. The Demography Minor is available to all Cornell undergraduates. It is offered by the Cornell Population Center in conjunction with the Department of Global Development, and the Department of Policy Analysis and Management.

The minor in Design and Environmental Analysis (D+EA) provides students with a lens for understanding the complex interactions between people and their physical environments. Students in the minor will have the opportunity to develop skills in design thinking, human-centered design, and evidence-based design. The D+EA minor allows students to flexibly explore a range of D+EA content through three key areas: Design Innovation + Strategy, Sustainable Futures, and Health + Well-being. The D+EA minor is an excellent complement to a number of majors across campus including business, global and public health, policy analysis and management, communication, information science, computer science, engineering, architecture, and real estate.

The Design Innovation and Strategy minor provides a comprehensive curriculum that teaches the fundamental processes of design thinking, and the application of human-centered design to the development and launch of a commercially-viable new venture. The minor leverages the world-class education of the College of Human Ecology’s Design and Environmental Analysis Department, the Samuel Curtis Johnson College of Business, and the College of Engineering. It prepares students for a variety of roles in business, non-profits and entrepreneurial endeavors. Students will come away from the curriculum understanding human needs; how to create, develop and deliver products, services, and experiences to meet those needs; and how to strategically launch those products and services into the marketplace.

ProgramName: Dyson Business Minor for Life Sciences
Description:
The Dyson Business Minor for Life Sciences (DBMLS) is geared toward students with a life sciences background who want to supplement their studies with a strong foundation in business management, and who are interested in a career in the life sciences industry.

The DBMLS is structured to provide students with a solid introduction to the language of business while emphasizing topics that are particularly relevant to the life sciences industry. Students complete five core business courses and one life sciences industry elective. The courses in the DBMLS are taught by Dyson faculty with extensive business experience and are offered online to accommodate students with demanding class and lab schedules.

The minor in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences is for students who are interested in the fundamentals of how the Earth works, and who wish to have this recognized on their transcript. The emphasis is on the interdisciplinary nature of the subject and the interactions between the atmosphere, oceans, and solid earth. The minor is flexible enough to accommodate both students with a strong background in math and science and students with less quantitative preparation. The minor is especially appropriate for students in other science and engineering fields who want to broaden their knowledge of Earth systems, as well as for students who want a science concentration but are not majoring in a science or engineering discipline. The department has five areas of concentration: geology, atmospheric science, environmental geosciences, ocean sciences, and climate change.

The East Asian Studies minor is designed for students who are interested in East Asia and would like to build a basic foundation for understanding the region, but do not have the time to commit to the East Asia Studies major. The minor may be pursued along with any major in any college. The minor is a great way for STEM and other professional school students to pursue a passion in the humanities and social sciences while broadening their global perspectives. The requirements for the minor are structured for students to gain a breadth of knowledge through introductory courses and a depth of understanding through upper-level coursework.

The Education Minor provides a university-wide undergraduate minor that enables students from a variety of majors to study education from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Students in the minor will achieve an understanding of education as a complex and multidimensional institution, and of its central place in modern society. We offer courses with perspectives from across the campus, including those in developmental psychology, sociology, history, and policy analysis.

Students will demonstrate an ability to:

Recognize the breadth of factors that influence education and human development.
Examine educational theory and practice from multiple disciplinary perspectives.
Critically analyze educational policy and practice.
Appreciate the importance of inquiry and reflection in promoting effective teaching and learning.
Communicate effectively in a variety of contexts.

The Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) minor is available to all undergraduates in the College of Engineering, and to students in other colleges who are majoring in a technical field. The ECE minor is particularly appropriate for students in other engineering majors who wish to broaden their horizons, for students in other technical fields (such as physics, mathematics, and computer science) who want to learn about the engineering applications of their science, and for students who are simply interested in the exciting field of ECE. The ECE minor curriculum is designed to provide a general overview of the field, so it is flexible. Students may choose courses in a number of areas of ECE or may concentrate on one or two. There are three components to the ECE minor: ECE foundation courses, ECE core courses, and ECE electives. These must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C or better must be received.

The Engineering Communications Program (ECP) offers a minor in engineering communications. The minor is designed for students who are interested in developing their communication skills. The minor helps students to learn how to communicate effectively about engineering and technical subjects to a wide range of audiences, from the general public to professional engineers. Students in the minor will also learn to work more effectively in teams and to take on leadership roles.

The Engineering Entrepreneurship minor, open to all undergraduate students in the College of Engineering, provides students an opportunity to build on their technical education with a structured curriculum to better understand the process of technology-based entrepreneurship. Many engineering students are interested in starting companies, or joining start-ups, upon graduation. The minor will help students develop business and entrepreneurial skills to translate technical inventions into commercial ventures. Students will learn the process of evaluating the commercial potential of a technology, developing a business plan and launching a new company.
