The Engineering Management Minor is a new minor in the College of Engineering that may be of particular interest to students in the College of Engineering and other Cornell colleges who want to combine their primary technical discipline with a set of courses designed to provide them with the management and leadership skills needed for their careers. A key goal of the minor is to develop leaders for a technical world. In an effort to keep the minor as accessible to as many students as possible, it has been designed to satisfy requirements for other minors and majors, where possible.

The English minor offers undergraduates the opportunity to study and practice the arts of literary interpretation and writing. Students who minor in English learn about a wide variety of literatures in English, their historical and cultural contexts, and the critical methods by which they can be understood. They work closely with a renowned faculty to develop their own critical and analytical voices and to hone their skills as writers.

The minor in Entomology provides a strong background in the science of entomology and a broader appreciation of the fascinating and important roles that insects play in the earth’s ecosystems. A minor in Entomology can prepare students for a diversity of career paths, including pest management, conservation and environmental biology, toxicology, apiculture, and human or veterinary medicine.

The cross-campus undergraduate Minor in Entrepreneurship and Innovation provides students in any major with the opportunity to study the vital processes of entrepreneurship and innovation, complementing the academic content of their majors and adding a dimension of practice to their university education. The goal of the minor is to provide students with the knowledge and skills to become entrepreneurs or ‘intrapreneurs’ (innovators within large organizations). The minor requires a sequence of courses and a significant team-based experience focused on the development of an innovative product, service or venture.

Concentration: Environmental Biology & Applied Ecology, Environmental & Resource Economics, Environmental Humanities, Environmental Policy & Governance, Land, Air & Water Resources, Sustainable Food & Agricultural Systems
Description: The environment and sustainability (E&S) minor is an opportunity for undergraduate students from any college at Cornell to develop a transdisciplinary understanding of environmental and sustainability issues. The minor is structured to help students become literate and critical thinkers with respect to the complex interplay between human and natural systems. Through a core course, a set of distribution requirements, an area of concentration in a specific subject area, and a capstone experience, students are challenged to integrate different disciplinary approaches to address a range of pressing environmental and sustainability challenges. The minor is designed to be accessible to all students, regardless of their major, and to provide opportunities to engage with world-class faculty from across the university who share a common interest in the environment and sustainability. Students who complete the minor will have a credential that demonstrates their commitment to and knowledge of environment and sustainability.

The Environmental Engineering Minor provides an opportunity for all Cornell undergraduates to learn about the scientific, engineering, and economic foundations of environmental engineering and to apply that knowledge to current environmental challenges. The minor has a flexible structure that allows students to select courses in one or more focus areas of interest, including environmental processes, environmental systems, and sustainable energy systems.

The minor in European studies, offered by the Institute for European Studies (IES) as part of the Mario Einaudi Center for International Studies, provides a coherent structure for students with an interest in the languages, cultures, and societies of Europe.

The minor is designed for students in any of Cornell’s undergraduate colleges who have a special interest in European studies. The minor helps students to craft a coherent program of study of Europe from the existing university curriculum. Students pursuing the minor will work with a member of the European studies faculty in their college to design a curriculum that is appropriate to their interests and major field of study. Upon graduating, students will have the European studies minor designated on their official transcript.

The undergraduate minor in Fashion Studies offers students a multi-disciplinary approach to study the history, material culture, design and contemporary business of fashion. Students will complete a required foundation course, FSAD 1140 - Introduction to Fashion Design, as well as a selection of courses from a pre-approved list spanning across art, anthropology, design, economics, fiber science, history, management and sociology. The minor is offered to all undergraduate students in all colleges. It is administered by the Department of Fiber Science and Apparel Design. Students must apply to be in the minor, ideally by the first semester of their junior year. Students are responsible for fulfilling all prerequisites for the listed courses. Students are also responsible for determining if the courses selected for the minor may be used to fulfill college/major requirements. Admission to the minor requires a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0. Interested students must meet with an FSAD advisor to be accepted into the minor. It is important to meet with the advisor early in academic career to plan the program of study and ensure all requirements can be met. Students must complete a minimum of 18 credits for the minor.

The FGSS minor offers students an interdisciplinary opportunity to study gender and sexuality. The minor provides a broad overview of the study of gender and sexuality as well as an opportunity to focus on a particular area of interest. Coursework in FGSS is grounded in the humanities and social sciences and draws from other fields as well, including the visual arts, biological sciences, and law. Students who minor in FGSS take a total of five courses. At least one of these five courses must be at the 3000-level or higher. Students are encouraged to choose a course of study that reflects their own interests, in consultation with the Director of Undergraduate Studies. All courses must be passed with a letter grade of C or better. Only courses listed in the FGSS course offerings may be used for the minor, unless an exception is granted by the Director of Undergraduate Studies. The S/U option is not available for any course that is to be counted toward the minor. A maximum of two courses from a student’s major may be used for the FGSS minor. All courses used for the minor must be taken for a letter grade. We do not accept study abroad credits, transfer credits, or First-Year Writing Seminars as part of the minor.

The Fiber Science minor offers students an opportunity to study the physical, chemical, and engineering properties of fibrous materials and their applications, which range from advanced engineering composites, to biomedical implants and fabrics for protective clothing. Through a sequence of core courses, students will gain a fundamental understanding of polymers, fibers, and the chemistry and physics of materials. Technical electives will offer students the opportunity to gain breadth in engineering, chemistry, and the applied sciences.

The film minor offers undergraduates an interdisciplinary curriculum in the history, theory, and criticism of film and other moving-image media. Students who complete the minor will gain a critical and historical understanding of the cinematic medium, including its relationship to culture, society, and other art forms. They will also learn a variety of analytical and interpretive skills for the study of film. The minor provides a strong complement to majors in the humanities and social sciences.

The film minor is administered by the Department of Performing and Media Arts.

The Department of Art offers a minor in fine arts. The minor in fine arts provides students with a strong foundation in the practice, history, and theory of art. Students must be on track to complete at least 18 credits with a grade of C or better to complete the minor.

The Food and Agricultural Business minor provides students with core business management and marketing principles, and an understanding of the structure and institutions of the food and agricultural sectors of the economy. It is intended for students who are interested in careers in the food and agricultural industries, from production agriculture through food processing and distribution. Students from a wide variety of majors find this minor a valuable complement to their studies. The minor requires 18 credits, including 6 credits of core courses and at least 12 credits of business management and marketing electives. Many of the business management and marketing electives have prerequisites that are part of the core requirements.

The Food Science minor is available to all Cornell undergraduate students. This minor is not available to Food Science majors. The minor provides students with a substantive understanding of the scientific principles involved in food processing, preservation, and safety. This is accomplished through a defined set of core food science courses that include food chemistry, food engineering, food microbiology, food safety, and sensory evaluation. Students are then able to select from a diverse set of elective courses to focus on areas of specific interest. Examples include dairy science, food fermentations, food quality, food law, food product development, and nutrition.

The minor in French offers students the opportunity to combine an interest in French and francophone language, literature, and culture with their major in another field. Courses for the minor taken in the Department of Romance Studies must be taught in French. No more than one course may be taken with a non-Cornell program abroad. No more than two courses may be taken at another institution (including Cornell- or non-Cornell-sponsored programs abroad).

The French minor consists of five courses (of at least 3 credits) in French language, literature, or culture at the 2000 level or above. No more than two courses at the 2000 level can be counted toward the minor. Of the five courses, at least three must be taken at Cornell. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and completed with a grade of C or better. AP credit may not be used to fulfill the requirements of the minor.

The Fungal Biology Minor is intended for students who have an interest in fungi and their roles in the environment, in causing plant and animal diseases, and in industrial applications. Students will develop a basic knowledge of fungi and will supplement this with courses in a selected area of specialization. Through this minor, students will have an opportunity to interact with the more than twenty-five faculty at Cornell University with whom they have common interests.

The undergraduate minor in Game Design is for students who are interested in the design, development, and study of games. The minor is highly interdisciplinary and provides students with a broad understanding of the field, as well as an opportunity to focus on a particular area of interest. The Game Design Initiative at Cornell is a collaboration of faculty from the College of Arts & Sciences, the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Engineering, and the College of Architecture, Art, and Planning. The program is administered by the Game Design Initiative in the Department of Computer Science.

The German Studies minor is designed for students who are interested in developing a fuller understanding of the culture of the German-speaking world. The minor provides a structure for students from all colleges and majors to develop a course of study that combines the acquisition of German language skills with the study of German literature, culture, history, and politics. Recent minors have combined their work in German Studies with majors in a wide range of fields from across the university: chemistry, biology, physics, government, history, music, hotel administration, industrial and labor relations, etc.

The Gerontology Minor provides a multidisciplinary approach to the study of the aging process and the life course. Gerontology draws on research from all the social and behavioral sciences, the biological sciences, and the humanities. Courses provide a broad understanding of the field and permit students to develop a focus on a particular aspect of aging. Students will work with the directors to develop a curriculum that best meets their interests and career goals. Students completing the minor will have a basic understanding of the demography of aging, life course development, and policy issues relevant to older adults. This basic understanding provides a strong foundation for students who plan to pursue a career that involves working with older adults or who have a personal interest in understanding aging.

The Global Asia minor introduces students to the study of modern Asia (East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia) as a dynamic and interconnected region of the world. Students in the minor gain a nuanced understanding of Asia’s rich and diverse histories, cultures, and political economies as well as the historical and contemporary flows of people, goods, and ideas that connect Asia with other parts of the world. The minor has an expansive intellectual vision that encourages students to think about Asia from a variety of disciplinary and methodological perspectives. The minor is administered by the Department of Asian Studies, but it is open to all Cornell undergraduates. It is an ideal course of study for students who want to develop an intellectual focus on Asia in addition to their major and for students who want to develop regional expertise for their future careers.

The Global Health Minor is an undergraduate program for students interested in learning about the complex social, economic, political, environmental, and cultural dimensions of health and disease. The minor is open to students from all Cornell colleges. The program is an academic, educational minor, and is not a pre-medical or pre-health program. The program does not grant a professional certificate or license.

The Great Books Minor provides a structured way for students to engage with some of the most influential works of the Western tradition. It invites students to reflect on the meaning of tradition, canonicity, and “greatness” itself. The purpose of the Minor is to encourage students to read important and challenging books in a variety of fields and to do so in a structured, thoughtful, and interdisciplinary way.

We are living in a time of unprecedented specialization, and so it is more important than ever to have a general and well-rounded education. The Great Books Minor offers such an opportunity. It is a supplement, not a rival, to a student’s major. The Minor works particularly well with majors from all the colleges. It allows students a way to make their Cornell education more coherent, more thoughtful, and more integrated.

The Healthy Futures minor is an interdisciplinary undergraduate minor that provides students with a solid foundation to understand and address pressing challenges and opportunities in population health. The minor offers a cohesive curriculum for students who wish to learn about the complex interplay of factors that influence population health locally and globally. It will prepare students to approach health issues from multiple disciplinary perspectives and work with diverse teams to develop solutions for a healthier world.

Students will learn to think critically about the social, environmental, ethical, and policy contexts of population health. They will also gain a foundational understanding of the biological and behavioral determinants of health, and the analytic tools used to evaluate health and health disparities. With a focus on experiential learning, the minor also offers opportunities for students to connect their academic coursework with health related problems and issues in the real-world.

The Hebrew minor, offered by the Department of Near Eastern Studies in the College of Arts and Sciences, helps students to attain a high level of proficiency in all language skills, as well as to become acquainted with the culture (literature, history, religion, politics, etc.) of which the language is a part. Students choosing this minor will have an excellent opportunity to focus their studies on Hebrew and acquire deep knowledge of the specific area that interests them.

The history minor consists of any five history courses, with the following stipulations: at least one course must be in U.S. history; at least one course must be in the history of a country or region other than the U.S. or Europe; at least one course must be in pre-modern history (before 1800); at least one course must be a 4000-level seminar. Cornell in Washington courses and one First-Year Writing Seminar taught by a member of the History Department may be used to fulfill the requirements of the minor. Transfer students may apply up to two history courses from their previous institution toward the minor with the approval of the Director of Undergraduate Studies.

The minor in history of art provides an introduction to the history of art and a deeper grounding in a particular area of interest. It is a good option for students who discover the history of art late in their Cornell careers or for those who want to devote the bulk of their undergraduate coursework to a different field but still maintain a connection to the study of art and its history.

The Horticulture minor is intended for students whose primary academic interests lie in other fields. The minor provides students with a way to organize a series of related courses that can provide a foundation in the science and art of horticulture. The School of Integrative Plant Science offers more than 50 courses in horticulture appropriate for both majors and non-majors.

The Human Development minor provides a structured opportunity for students majoring in other areas to gain a basic foundation in the theories, research findings, and methods of human development from a truly interdisciplinary perspective. The field of human development focuses on how people develop over the entire lifespan in their social, cultural, and historical contexts. As such, the study of human development integrates theory and research from a range of disciplines, including psychology, sociology, biology, and neuroscience. The minor provides a strong background for students considering a wide range of careers including medicine, law, public policy, social work, education, and business.

The Inequality Studies Minor, housed in the Center for the Study of Inequality, is an interdisciplinary program designed for students interested in the systematic study of social and economic inequality. The minor is open to students in all Cornell undergraduate colleges. The curriculum is structured to provide students with a broad understanding of the causes and consequences of inequality, as well as the social, economic, and political responses to it. The minor introduces students to the core subject matter of inequality studies; exposes them to a wide range of analytical and methodological approaches; and deepens their understanding of a particular substantive area of inequality studies.

The minor in Infectious Disease Biology provides an interdisciplinary program of study for students interested in infectious diseases of public health importance, including those that are zoonotic (transmitted from animals to humans) and food-borne. Students take foundational courses in biology and microbiology and then elect further courses in a variety of disciplines including entomology, food science, microbiology, immunology, and animal science. The course of study is designed to provide students with a strong background in the biology of infectious agents and their hosts and with an appreciation of the complex factors that influence the transmission and maintenance of disease-causing agents in a population. Students also gain a broader perspective through the study of socioeconomic and policy factors that are critical to the prevention and control of infectious diseases.

The Information Science Minor provides a coherent program of study in the emerging interdisciplinary field of Information Science. The minor is available to all undergraduate students in all colleges at Cornell. The minor requires the student to complete a core of three courses in Information Science and a set of three electives from an approved list. These electives must form a coherent plan of study, approved by an Information Science faculty advisor.

The minor in International Development (ID) offers a coherent academic focus for undergraduates interested in the challenges of development in low-income countries. The complexity of these issues requires an interdisciplinary approach that encompasses the natural and social sciences. Students are expected to acquire a broad-based knowledge of development issues from a cross-disciplinary perspective and at the same time focus on one particular area in greater depth. The minor is intended to expand students’ understanding of the problems of international development and how they might be addressed.

Concentration: International Political Economy, International Law and Organizations, Foreign Policy and Diplomatic History, International and Comparative Politics, Culture, Transnationalism, and Globalization
Description: The minor in international relations (IR) provides an interdisciplinary program in the study of global affairs. It is designed for students with career and vocational interests in international affairs, including international development and humanitarian assistance, international law and diplomacy, international business and finance, and international security. The minor introduces students to the crucial issues of our time–from global climate change to poverty, trade, and war and peace. The IR minor is not an independent major, but it can be taken in conjunction with any Cornell major. It is housed in the Government Department, but it is open to all students, regardless of college or major.

The minor in International Trade and Development provides students with a framework for understanding the economic relationships among countries, the-institutions that govern these relationships, and the role of trade and other economic policies in promoting development and alleviating poverty.

The Italian studies minor (which is administered by the Department of Romance Studies) is designed to give students a broad understanding of Italian culture. In addition to a solid linguistic foundation, the minor offers an introduction to the rich and diverse cultural production of Italy from the Middle Ages to the present day. It represents a flexible program that can be easily combined with a variety of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences.

The Jewish Studies Minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to the study of Jewish culture, history, and literature from antiquity to the present. The minor is open to students in all colleges of the university.

The minor consists of five courses for a total of at least 20 credits, chosen from the Jewish studies course list. Of the five required courses:

1. Two must be from the following core courses: JWST 1500, JWST 1700/NES 1700, JWST 2644/NES 2644, and JWST 2720/NES 2720.
2. One course must be at the 3000- or 4000-level.
3. One course must be in the pre-modern period, and one in the modern period (a single course may not be used to fulfill both requirements).
4. A single course can be used to fulfill up to two requirements (e.g., JWST 2644 can fulfill both a core course and a pre-modern requirement).
5. One of the courses must be chosen from the approved list of Jewish Studies courses and can be counted towards the student’s major. The other four courses must be taken outside the student’s major or in a different department from the major (in the case of interdisciplinary majors, this means the four courses must not be cross-listed with any other courses counting towards the major). This requirement may be waived at the discretion of the director of undergraduate studies.
6. All courses for the minor must be taken for a letter grade.

All courses to be used for the minor must be approved in writing by the director of undergraduate studies.

The minor in landscape studies is intended for undergraduates who want to become more knowledgeable about the history, theory, and practice of landscape design and land-use planning. The landscape is a dynamic medium that records and expresses natural and cultural processes, and it reflects our values and attitudes toward the environment and toward the land itself. Landscape studies may therefore range in scale from a garden to a continent. The minor offers both a descriptive and a normative view of landscapes, and in a creative and intellectual manner, it encourages students to critically examine issues of nature, design, culture, and place. It also enables students to better understand the ways in which human beings have created and managed the landscapes we inhabit. The minor is offered by the Department of Landscape Architecture in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

The Latin American and Caribbean Studies (LACS) Program offers a university-wide undergraduate minor in Latin American and Caribbean Studies. The LACS minor is designed for students in any of the seven Cornell undergraduate colleges who have a special interest in the region. The LACS minor provides a structured, yet flexible, way to study Latin America and the Caribbean from a variety of disciplinary perspectives. The minor is especially suitable for students who anticipate a career in which a knowledge of the region and its languages is a significant asset. It allows students to focus some of their elective coursework on a fascinating and important part of the world, and to be recognized for it. The minor also helps students prepare for graduate study in Latin American and Caribbean Studies or other international fields.

The Latina/o Studies Program (LSP) Minor is an interdisciplinary program that provides students with a scholarly foundation in the study of Latina/o history, culture, and experience. The minor allows for an in-depth study of the historical trajectories and contemporary lives of Latina/os in the United States and their diasporic communities throughout the Americas. Through a range of courses in the humanities and social sciences, the curriculum examines topics such as racialization, immigration, colonialism, expressive cultures, language, and gender and sexuality.

The Law and Society minor is an interdisciplinary program that allows students to develop a rich, integrated understanding of the social, political, economic, and cultural functions of law. Law and Society scholars use the methods of the social sciences and humanities to study law as a social institution.

The Law and Society minor gives students a framework for understanding legal institutions, rules, and processes, and their relationship to social and historical contexts. It also provides a strong foundation for students considering law school or other graduate programs, as well as those interested in careers in public service, policy, and other law-related professions.

ProgramName: Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, & Transgender Studies Minor
Description: The Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) Studies minor provides an interdisciplinary and scholarly framework for the study of sexuality. Drawing on disciplines in the humanities and social sciences, as well as the natural sciences, the minor in LGBT Studies examines the history, the social and political life, and the creative expressions of lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people. Courses in the minor analyze the formation of sexual identities; the role of sexuality in the arts, in the media, in science, and in the law; the closet and its consequences; the intersections of sexuality, race, class, and gender; the lives of sexual minorities in the United States and in other cultures; and the achievements of LGBT civil rights movements. Students with a minor in LGBT Studies will be able to apply the critical thinking, reading, writing, and analytical skills fostered by a liberal arts education to a specific and developing field of knowledge. Students minoring in LGBT Studies are required to take one core course, LGBT 2290 - Introduction to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Studies, and four additional courses from the list of LGBT Studies courses in the catalog. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C or better must be received in all minor courses. Courses are selected by the student in consultation with their LGBT Studies faculty advisor. The advisor is chosen by the student from the list of LGBT Studies faculty.

The linguistics minor provides a systematic introduction to the study of human language. Its core consists of three courses that together provide an overview of the main subfields of the discipline: phonology (the study of speech sounds), syntax (the study of sentence structure), and either semantics (the study of meaning) or historical linguistics (the study of language change and the history and development of languages). Further courses may be chosen according to a student’s own interests, and may focus on a variety of topics, including the language of a particular geographical area, computational linguistics, language and society, and animal communication. An understanding of linguistics is highly relevant to students with an interest in human cognition (psychology, philosophy, anthropology), in literature and the humanities, in computer science, and in the study of specific foreign languages. Students minoring in linguistics are encouraged to take courses in a variety of languages, since an appreciation of the diversity of human language is central to the field. Many courses in various language departments may be used to satisfy some of the requirements for the minor. Students should select these courses in consultation with their minor advisor, to ensure a coherent program of study that familiarizes them with the different ways in which human languages can vary, as well as in more distantly related languages.

The Materials Science and Engineering (MSE) minor provides a coherent program of study for students who want a strong background in materials science and engineering but are majoring in another field. The minor requires a minimum of six courses. Three of these must be from the MSE Core Curriculum: MSE 2610, MSE 2620, and MSE 3010. Two more must be chosen from a specific list of MSE senior-level courses. The final requirement is one additional MSE course that is not a special-project course. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C- or better must be achieved in each course.

The Mathematics Minor is designed to give students a strong background in mathematics, which is useful for graduate study in many fields. Students considering the Mathematics Minor should consult a faculty member in the Department of Mathematics. To be admitted to the minor, students should complete the application form available at the department office or on the department website. Students must complete all minor requirements by their graduation date. In some cases, courses may be used to satisfy requirements for both a major and a minor.

The Mechanical Engineering minor is intended for students who are not majoring in mechanical engineering but who are interested in the field. The minor provides students with an introduction to the core areas of mechanical engineering, including mechanics, materials, thermal sciences, and design. The minor is flexible, allowing students to tailor their course selection to their specific interests.

The undergraduate minor in Media Studies, housed in the Department of Performing and Media Arts, is an interdisciplinary program that includes courses in a wide variety of departments. The minor offers students the opportunity to study the history, theory, and practice of a wide range of media forms. Students learn to think critically about media as cultural and aesthetic forms that are linked to particular social, political, and economic contexts. The minor aims to provide students with a broad understanding of different media (print, radio, film, television, video, digital media) and to familiarize them with a range of analytical and theoretical approaches to media studies. The interdisciplinary nature of the minor encourages students to consider media from multiple perspectives and to develop a comparative framework for their study.

The undergraduate minor in Medieval Studies is a multidisciplinary program that offers a coherent and comprehensive, yet flexible, program for students who wish to pursue a special interest in the culture of the Middle Ages. The minor can attractively supplement a major in such fields as classics, history, languages and literatures, philosophy, or religious studies. The requirements for the minor are sufficiently flexible to accommodate a wide variety of interests and needs—from the student who is just beginning to explore a new field to the one who is already planning graduate work in a medieval specialization. Each student’s program is planned in consultation with the Director of Undergraduate Studies, with whom all interested students are urged to discuss their plans. Students complete five courses from a variety of offerings in Art History, Classics, Comparative Literature, English, German Studies, History, Music, Near Eastern Studies, Philosophy, Religious Studies, and Romance Studies.

The Minor in Microbiology is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the roles that microorganisms play in the natural world and in human affairs. The minor provides a strong foundation in the fundamental principles of microbiology, including microbial physiology, genetics, and diversity, as well as opportunities for more specialized study in areas such as microbial pathogenesis, environmental microbiology, and biotechnology. Students in the minor will also develop practical skills in laboratory techniques and data analysis. The minor prepares students for a variety of careers in fields such as medicine, public health, biotechnology, and environmental science, as well as for advanced study in microbiology and related disciplines.

The undergraduate minor in migration studies, open to students in all Cornell undergraduate colleges, provides a framework for students to pursue a comprehensive, interdisciplinary course of study of migration. The core courses of the minor provide a firm grounding in the historical, political, economic, social and cultural dimensions of migration and its consequences. From that base, students build an individualized course of study, drawing from a rich menu of migration-related courses taught by faculty from across the university and relevant off-campus study programs. The minor is administered by the Migrations initiative.

ProgramName: Minority, Indigenous, and Third World Studies Minor
Description: The Minority, Indigenous, and Third World Studies (MITWS) undergraduate minor, housed in the Cornell Center for Social Sciences, is a LSA-affiliated program that offers an interdisciplinary curriculum to students interested in the histories, cultures, and socioeconomic and political conditions of marginalized and subaltern peoples in the U.S. and around the world. The curriculum in MITWS places a strong emphasis on the politics of race, ethnicity, indigeneity, and diaspora. By taking a comparative and global approach to the study of social marginalization, the MITWS minor encourages students to critically examine the production and articulation of racial and ethnic identities, and the structural and institutional bases of inequality and oppression. The curriculum for the minor is designed to provide students with the critical and analytical tools to engage with a variety of social and cultural issues, including racial and ethnic formations, indigenous sovereignty and rights, migration and displacement, colonialism and post-colonialism, and social justice and human rights. Students pursuing the minor must complete an introductory course, four elective courses and a senior seminar. Students are encouraged to consult with the MITWS faculty in designing a curriculum that is tailored to their specific intellectual interests, and in choosing an advisor for the senior seminar paper. For the most up to date information and course listings, see the program website at lsp.cornell.edu/minority-indigenous-and-third-world-studies, or contact the Program Manager as well as the MITWS Program Director.

The minor in Near Eastern studies is designed to provide undergraduate students with a general knowledge and understanding of the cultures, civilizations, languages, and literatures of the Near East from antiquity to the modern day. The minor is sufficiently flexible to accommodate a wide variety of student interests and to be easily combined with a number of different majors.

ProgramName: Operations Research and Management Science Minor
Science Communication and Public Engagement Minor
